text: A shopkeeper marks an article 40% above its cost price and then allows a discount of 15% on the marked price. What is his profit percentage?
solution: Let CP = 100. Marked price = 140.
Selling price = 140 × 0.85 = 119.
fast: Net multiplier = 1.40 × 0.85 = 1.19 → 19% profit.
hint: Convert both changes into multiplying factors.
trap: Adding 40 − 15 = 25% ignores that the discount is on the larger marked price.
note: Successive % changes multiply: (1 + a)(1 − b) − 1.

text: The price of sugar rises by 25%. By what percentage must a family reduce its sugar consumption so that its expenditure on sugar does not change?
solution: Expenditure = price × quantity. New price = 1.25 × old.
To keep expenditure constant, quantity must become 1/1.25 = 0.8 of old.
Reduction = 20%.
fast: Increase of 1/4 ⇒ reduction of 1/(4+1) = 1/5 = 20%.
trap: Answering 25% (the same number) is the classic trap.
note: If price rises by 1/n, consumption falls by 1/(n+1).

text: A person's salary is first increased by 20%, then decreased by 20%, and finally increased by 10%. What is the net percentage change in the salary?
options: No change
solution: Net change = +5.6%.
trap: Assuming +20% and −20% cancel; they leave a 4% loss.
note: +x% then −x% always gives a net fall of x²/100 %.

text: A trader sells two articles at ₹990 each. On one he gains 10% and on the other he loses 10%. What is his overall loss in rupees?
options: No profit, no loss
solution: First article: CP = 990/1.1 = 900.
Second article: CP = 990/0.9 = 1100.
Total CP = 2000, total SP = 1980. Loss = ₹20.
fast: Same SP with ±x% ⇒ loss% = x²/100 = 1% of total CP (2000) = ₹20.
trap: Thinking gain and loss cancel. They do not when the SPs are equal.
note: Equal SP, gain x% and loss x% ⇒ always a net loss of x²/100 %.

text: A dealer sells rice at 5% below the cost price, but uses a weight of 800 g in place of 1 kg. What is his actual profit percentage?
solution: Let the cost of 1 kg be ₹100.
For each 'kg' sold he charges ₹95 but hands over only 800 g, which costs him ₹80.
fast: Profit% = (Price received − True cost)/True cost = (95 − 80)/80.
hint: Compare the money received with the cost of the goods actually delivered.
trap: Using 1000 g as the base (15%) instead of the 800 g actually delivered.
note: False weights: true cost = (weight given/weight claimed) × CP.

text: The population of a town is 50,000. It increases by 10% in the first year, decreases by 10% in the second year and increases by 20% in the third year. What is the population at the end of the third year?
trap: Adding the rates (+20%) gives 60,000.
note: Population/depreciation chains are successive-percentage problems.

text: When an article is sold at a 20% discount on its marked price, the seller makes a 12% profit. What would be his profit percentage if he sold it at a 10% discount instead?
solution: At 10% discount: SP = 0.9 × 1.4 C = 1.26 C.
Profit = 26%.
hint: First find the marked price as a multiple of the cost price.
trap: Assuming a 10-point drop in discount adds exactly 10 points of profit (22%).
note: Link MP and CP through SP: MP × (1 − d) = CP × (1 + p).

text: What is the difference between the compound interest (compounded annually) and the simple interest on ₹10,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum?
solution: Difference = ₹100.
hint: The extra is interest earned on the first year's interest.
trap: Computing CI for 2 years as 2 × 1,000 + 1,000 (overcounting).
note: 2-year CI − SI = P·r²; 3-year = P·r²(3 + r).

text: A sum of money doubles itself in 5 years at simple interest. In how many years will it become four times itself at the same rate?
solution: Doubling ⇒ interest = 100% of P in 5 years ⇒ rate = 20% p.a.
Four times ⇒ interest = 300% of P ⇒ 300/20 = 15 years.
fast: SI grows linearly: 1× interest in 5 years ⇒ 3× interest in 15 years.
hint: Four times the sum means interest is three times the sum.
trap: Answering 10 years (thinking 4× = 2 doublings as in CI) or 20 years (4 × 5).
note: SI: n-fold amount needs (n − 1) × P interest.

text: A sum invested at compound interest (compounded annually) amounts to ₹12,100 in 2 years and ₹13,310 in 3 years. What is the principal?
fast: Ratio of consecutive amounts = 1 + r; divide back twice.
hint: Divide the 3-year amount by the 2-year amount.
trap: Using the difference ₹1,210 as SI for one year on the principal.
note: Consecutive CI amounts form a GP with ratio (1 + r).

text: A loan of ₹21,000 at 10% per annum compound interest is repaid in two equal instalments at the end of the first and second years. What is the value of each instalment (in ₹)?
solution: Present value of instalments must equal the loan: x/1.1 + x/1.21 = 21,000.
hint: Discount each instalment back to today.
trap: Dividing 21,000 × 1.21 by 2 (ignores interest on reducing balance).
note: Equal instalments: P = Σ x/(1 + r)^k.

text: If A : B = 3 : 4 and B : C = 6 : 7, then A : B : C is
solution: Make B common: A:B = 9:12, B:C = 12:14.
fast: LCM of B-terms (4, 6) = 12; scale both ratios.
trap: Writing 3:4:7 by simply joining the ratios.
note: Chain ratios by equalising the shared term.

text: ₹7,800 is divided among A, B and C such that 2A = 3B = 4C. What is C's share (in ₹)?
fast: Reciprocals of 2, 3, 4 ⇒ 6:4:3.
trap: Taking the ratio as 2:3:4 (direct instead of inverse).
note: pA = qB = rC ⇒ A:B:C = 1/p : 1/q : 1/r.

text: The cost of running a bus is partly fixed and partly proportional to the distance covered. A 100 km trip costs ₹5,000 and a 150 km trip costs ₹6,500. What will a 250 km trip cost?
solution: Let cost = F + k·d. 50 extra km cost 1,500 ⇒ k = 30/km.
fast: Cost is linear: each extra 50 km adds ₹1,500; 150 → 250 is two more steps: 6,500 + 3,000.
hint: Use the difference of the two trips to find the per-km part.
trap: Treating cost as directly proportional: 5,000 × 2.5 = 12,500.
note: Partly fixed + partly variable ⇒ straight line, not a proportion.

text: Two numbers are in the ratio 3 : 5. If 10 is added to each, the ratio becomes 5 : 7. What is the larger number?
solution: Larger number = 5k = 25.
fast: Difference is constant: 2k = 2m where new terms are 5m, 7m ⇒ 3k + 10 = 5k ⇒ k = 5.
hint: Adding the same number keeps the difference unchanged.
trap: Forgetting to multiply k back: answering 5.
note: Constant-difference trick: equate differences of the two ratios.

text: Six years ago the ratio of the ages of A and B was 3 : 4. Six years from now it will be 5 : 6. What is A's present age (in years)?
fast: Age difference k is constant: 3:4 → 5:6 means difference 1 part in both; gap 12 years = (5 − 3) parts ⇒ 1 part = 6.
hint: The difference in ages never changes.
trap: Stopping at k = 6 or giving A's age six years ago (18).
note: Age problems: work with the constant age gap.

text: The average of 11 numbers is 30. The average of the first six is 28 and the average of the last six is 33. What is the sixth number?
solution: Sum of first six = 168; last six = 198; all eleven = 330.
The sixth number is counted twice: 168 + 198 − 330 = 36.
fast: Deviation method: first six contribute −12, last six +18; sixth = 30 + (−12 + 18) = 36.
hint: Which number appears in both groups?
trap: Averaging 28 and 33.
note: Overlapping groups: overlap = sum(group1) + sum(group2) − total.

text: The average weight of 30 students is 50 kg. When the teacher's weight is included, the average rises by 0.5 kg. What is the teacher's weight (in kg)?
solution: Teacher = 65.5 kg.
fast: Teacher = old average + (new count × increase) = 50 + 31 × 0.5.
hint: The teacher must lift all 31 people by 0.5.
trap: Using 30 × 0.5 instead of 31 × 0.5 (gives 65).
note: New member = old avg + n_new × change.

text: The average of 10 distinct positive integers is 15. What is the maximum possible value of the largest of these integers?
solution: Sum = 150. To maximise the largest, make the other nine as small as possible and distinct: 1, 2, …, 9 (sum 45).
fast: Max one = total − minimum possible sum of the rest.
hint: The other nine must be distinct positive integers.
trap: Using 1 for all nine others (ignores 'distinct'), giving 141.
note: Extremal problems: push all other values to their bounds.

text: The average of five consecutive odd numbers is 27. What is the product of the smallest and the largest of these numbers?
solution: Middle number = average = 27. Numbers: 23, 25, 27, 29, 31.
hint: For evenly spaced numbers, the average is the middle term.
trap: Using spacing 1 instead of 2 (25 × 29 = 725).
note: Symmetric sets: a² − d² trick for extreme products.

text: In what ratio must rice costing ₹60/kg be mixed with rice costing ₹75/kg so that the mixture costs ₹65/kg?
fast: Distances from the mean are swapped: cheaper : dearer = 10 : 5.
trap: Writing 1:2 (not swapping the distances).
note: Alligation: ratio = (dear − mean) : (mean − cheap).

text: A 40-litre mixture of milk and water contains 25% water. How many litres of water must be added so that water becomes 40% of the new mixture?
options: 8 L
6 L
solution: Milk = 30 L (unchanged). In the new mixture milk is 60%.
New total = 30/0.6 = 50 L ⇒ water added = 10 L.
fast: Track the component that does not change (milk).
trap: Adding 15% of 40 = 6 L.
note: Keep the constant component fixed and rescale the total.

text: A vessel contains 80 L of pure milk. 8 L is removed and replaced with water. This operation is performed three times in all. How much milk (in litres) remains?
solution: Each operation keeps (1 − 8/80) = 0.9 of the milk.
fast: Repeated replacement: final = initial × (1 − x/V)ⁿ.
hint: What fraction of milk survives one operation?
trap: Subtracting 8 L three times (56 L).
note: Replacement formula works only when the removed quantity is equal each time.

text: Alloy A contains copper and zinc in the ratio 3 : 2 and alloy B contains them in the ratio 1 : 4. How many kg of alloy B must be mixed with 10 kg of alloy A so that the resulting alloy is 40% copper?
solution: Copper in A = 60%, in B = 20%.
Alligation around 40%: A : B = (40 − 20) : (60 − 40) = 1 : 1.
So B = 10 kg.
fast: Copper % 60 and 20, target 40 is exactly the midpoint ⇒ equal quantities.
hint: Convert each alloy to copper percentage.
trap: Working with zinc % on one side and copper % on the other.
note: Alligation works on the percentage of one chosen component.

text: A can finish a job in 12 days and B in 18 days. How many days will they take working together?
options: 7.2 days
15 days
7.5 days
8 days
solution: Combined rate = 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36 per day.
Time = 36/5 = 7.2 days.
fast: Product/sum = 12 × 18/30 = 7.2.
hint: Add the rates, not the times.
trap: Averaging the days (15).
note: Two workers: T = ab/(a + b).

text: A and B together finish a job in 12 days, B and C in 15 days, and C and A in 20 days. In how many days can A alone finish the job?
solution: Take total work = 60 units. A+B = 5, B+C = 4, C+A = 3 units/day.
A+B+C = 12/2 = 6 units/day.
A = 6 − (B+C) = 2 units/day ⇒ 60/2 = 30 days.
fast: LCM-units method avoids fractions.
hint: Add all three pair rates and halve.
trap: Forgetting to halve the sum of pair rates.
note: Pair-sum problems: total = (sum of pairs)/2.

text: Pipe A fills a tank in 20 minutes and pipe B in 30 minutes, while pipe C empties the full tank in 15 minutes. If all three are opened together on an empty tank, how long will it take to fill it?
options: 45 minutes
30 minutes
90 minutes
60 minutes
solution: Tank = 60 units. A = +3, B = +2, C = −4 units/min.
Net = +1 unit/min ⇒ 60 minutes.
fast: LCM 60 units; net rate +1.
hint: Treat the emptying pipe as negative work.
trap: Adding all three rates as positive.
note: Leak/outlet pipes carry a negative sign.

text: A and B together can complete a job in 12 days. They work together for 4 days, after which B leaves and A finishes the remaining work in 16 days. In how many days can B alone complete the job?
solution: In 4 days together they finish 4/12 = 1/3 of the job.
A does the remaining 2/3 in 16 days ⇒ A alone takes 24 days (rate 1/24).
fast: A's rate from the 'remaining work' step, then subtract from the joint rate.
hint: First find how much work was left when B left.
trap: Assuming A did the whole job in 16 days (rate 1/16).
note: Joint rate − known rate = unknown rate.

text: A can do a job in 20 days and B in 30 days. They start together, but A leaves 5 days before the job is completed. In how many days is the job completed in total?
solution: Let total time = t. B works t days, A works (t − 5).
fast: Pretend A works full time: extra work A would do in 5 days = 5/20 = 1/4. Combined rate 1/12 does 1 + 1/4 ⇒ t = 15.
hint: Write the work equation with t as total days.
trap: Subtracting 5 from the answer at the end (giving 10).
note: 'Leaves x days before completion' ⇒ that worker works (t − x).

text: A is twice as efficient as B. Together they finish a job in 14 days. How many days would A alone take?
fast: A does 2/3 of the combined work rate ⇒ 14 × 3/2 = 21.
hint: Efficiency is the rate of work.
trap: Answering 28 (doubling the days) or 7 (halving).
note: Efficiency ratio a:b ⇒ time ratio b:a.

text: A car travels to a place at 60 km/h and returns along the same road at 40 km/h. What is its average speed for the entire journey?
options: 45 km/h
50 km/h
52 km/h
48 km/h
solution: Average speed for equal distances = 2ab/(a + b) = 2 × 60 × 40/100 = 48 km/h.
fast: Harmonic mean of 60 and 40.
trap: Taking the arithmetic mean (50 km/h).
note: Equal distances ⇒ harmonic mean; equal times ⇒ arithmetic mean.

text: A 240 m long train crosses a pole in 12 seconds. How many seconds will it take to cross a 360 m long platform?
solution: Distance to cross platform = 240 + 360 = 600 m ⇒ 30 s.
fast: Time scales with length: 12 × 600/240 = 30.
hint: Crossing a platform means covering train + platform length.
trap: Using only 360 m (18 s).
note: Pole: distance = train length; platform: train + platform.

text: Two trains 150 m and 100 m long run on parallel tracks in opposite directions at 54 km/h and 36 km/h. How long do they take to cross each other completely?
solution: Relative speed = 54 + 36 = 90 km/h = 25 m/s.
trap: Subtracting speeds (as if same direction) gives 50 s.
note: km/h → m/s: multiply by 5/18.

text: A boat goes 24 km upstream and 28 km downstream in 6 hours. It goes 30 km upstream and 21 km downstream in 6.5 hours. What is the speed of the boat in still water (in km/h)?
solution: Let u = 1/(upstream speed), v = 1/(downstream speed).
Multiply the first by 3 and the second by 4: 72u + 84v = 18; 120u + 84v = 26 ⇒ 48u = 8 ⇒ u = 1/6.
28v = 6 − 4 = 2 ⇒ v = 1/14. Upstream = 6, downstream = 14 ⇒ boat = (6 + 14)/2 = 10.
fast: Treat reciprocals of speeds as the unknowns to keep the equations linear.
hint: Let the unknowns be the time per km upstream and downstream.
trap: Answering the stream speed (4) or a downstream speed (14).
note: Boat = (D + U)/2, stream = (D − U)/2.

text: In a 1 km race, A beats B by 100 m and B beats C by 100 m. By how many metres does A beat C?
solution: When A runs 1,000 m, B runs 900 m.
When B runs 1,000 m, C runs 900 m ⇒ when B runs 900 m, C runs 810 m.
A beats C by 1,000 − 810 = 190 m.
trap: Adding the margins (200 m).
note: Race margins chain multiplicatively.

text: P and Q are 90 km apart. Two cyclists start at the same time from P and Q towards each other at 20 km/h and 25 km/h respectively. After they meet, how many minutes does the cyclist from Q take to reach P?
solution: They meet after 90/45 = 2 hours, 40 km from P.
The Q-cyclist still has 40 km to P at 25 km/h ⇒ 1.6 h = 96 minutes.
fast: Remaining distance for Q-cyclist = distance covered by the other = 20 × 2.
trap: Reporting 1.6 or answering for the wrong cyclist (the P-cyclist needs 2.5 h).
note: After meeting, each covers what the other covered before meeting.

text: A and B start running from the same point on a 600 m circular track in the same direction at 5 m/s and 3 m/s. After how many seconds will they first meet again at the starting point?
solution: A completes a lap in 120 s and B in 200 s.
They are both at the start at common multiples: LCM(120, 200) = 600 s.
fast: Meeting at the start ⇒ LCM of lap times.
trap: Using the first meeting anywhere on the track (600/(5 − 3) = 300 s).
note: Meet anywhere: L/relative speed; meet at start: LCM of lap times.

text: Walking at 5 km/h a man reaches his office 10 minutes late; walking at 6 km/h he reaches 5 minutes early. What is the distance to the office (in km)?
solution: Time difference = 15 min = 1/4 h.
fast: d = (product of speeds/difference) × time gap = 30 × 1/4.
trap: Taking the gap as 5 minutes (10 − 5).
note: Two-speed problems: d = s₁s₂/(s₂ − s₁) × Δt.

text: 3 pens and 2 notebooks cost ₹110, while 2 pens and 3 notebooks cost ₹115. What is the cost of one notebook?
solution: Adding: 5p + 5n = 225 ⇒ p + n = 45.
Subtracting: n − p = 5.
fast: Add and subtract the equations instead of substituting.
hint: The equations are symmetric; use their sum and difference.
trap: Solving for the pen (₹20) and reporting it.
note: Symmetric linear pairs: add for the sum, subtract for the difference.

text: How many two-digit numbers are exactly four times the sum of their digits?
solution: a = 1, 2, 3, 4 give 12, 24, 36, 48 (a = 5 gives b = 10, invalid).
Answer: 4.
fast: Reduce to b = 2a and count the valid digits.
trap: Including a = 0 (not two-digit) or a = 5 (b = 10 is not a digit).
note: Digit problems: remember 1 ≤ a ≤ 9, 0 ≤ b ≤ 9.

text: A purse contains 50 coins, all of ₹1 and ₹2 denominations, with a total value of ₹74. How many ₹2 coins are there?
fast: If all were ₹1 coins the value would be 50; each ₹2 coin adds ₹1 extra ⇒ 24.
trap: Answering the ₹1 count (26).
note: Assumption method: excess value ÷ excess per item.

text: How many ordered pairs of non-negative integers (x, y) satisfy 2x + 3y = 30?
solution: 2x = 30 − 3y must be even and non-negative ⇒ y even, 0 ≤ y ≤ 10.
fast: y steps by 2 (coefficient of x) from 0 to 10.
hint: Which values of y keep 30 − 3y even?
trap: Excluding zero values (would give 4).
note: Solutions of ax + by = c step by b in x and a in y.

text: x, y and z are positive integers such that x + y + z = 12 and x + 2y + 3z = 20. How many ordered triples (x, y, z) are possible?
solution: Then x = 12 − y − z = 5, 6, 7, all positive.
(y, z) = (0, 4) is excluded because y must be positive. Answer: 3.
fast: Eliminate x immediately by subtracting.
hint: Subtract the first equation from the second.
trap: Counting (0, 4) and answering 4.
note: Always re-check positivity of the eliminated variable.

text: The sum of the present ages of a father and his son is 50 years. Five years ago the father was seven times as old as the son. What is the son's present age (in years)?
fast: Five years ago their ages summed to 40 in ratio 7:1 ⇒ son was 5, now 10.
hint: Look at the sum of ages five years ago.
trap: Reporting the son's age five years ago (5).
note: Shift the sum by the number of people × years.

text: How many integers x satisfy |x − 3| < 5?
solution: Integers −1 to 7 ⇒ 9 values.
fast: Open interval of width 10 around 3 contains 2 × 5 − 1 = 9 integers.
hint: Remove the modulus as a double inequality.
trap: Including the endpoints −2 and 8 (strict inequality).
note: |x − a| < b ⇔ a − b < x < a + b.

text: How many integer values of x satisfy x² − 7x + 10 < 0?
solution: Integers: 3, 4 ⇒ 2 values.
fast: Upward parabola is negative strictly between its roots.
trap: Including 2 and 5 where the expression is 0.
note: (x − a)(x − b) < 0 ⇒ between a and b.

text: What is the minimum value of |x − 1| + |x − 4| + |x − 10| over all real x?
solution: The sum of distances is minimised at the median point x = 4.
fast: Minimum of Σ|x − aᵢ| occurs at the median of the aᵢ.
hint: Think of distances on a number line.
trap: Using the mean (5): gives 4 + 1 + 5 = 10.
note: Sum of absolute deviations is minimised at the median.

text: How many ordered pairs of integers (x, y) satisfy |x| + |y| ≤ 3?
solution: For |x| = 0, 1, 2, 3, |y| can go up to 3, 2, 1, 0.
Count: x = 0 → 7; x = ±1 → 5 each; x = ±2 → 3 each; x = ±3 → 1 each.
fast: Lattice points in |x| + |y| ≤ n = 2n² + 2n + 1 = 25 for n = 3.
trap: Counting only the first quadrant and multiplying by 4 (double-counts the axes).
note: Diamond lattice count: 2n² + 2n + 1.

text: If x and y are positive real numbers with x + y = 10, what is the maximum value of x²y?
solution: Equality at x/2 = y = 10/3 ⇒ x = 20/3, y = 10/3.
fast: Split x into two equal halves so that all three parts can be equal.
trap: Setting x = y = 5 (gives 125, not the maximum).
note: For max xᵃyᵇ with x + y fixed: x : y = a : b.

text: The roots of x² − 5x + k = 0 differ by 1. What is k?
solution: Roots sum to 5 and differ by 1 ⇒ roots are 2 and 3.
k = product = 6.
hint: Use sum and difference of roots.
trap: Using (α − β) = 1 as (α − β)² = 1 without the 4k term correctly.
note: (α − β)² = (α + β)² − 4αβ.

text: If α and β are the roots of x² − 6x + 4 = 0, what is α² + β²?
fast: (sum)² − 2(product).
trap: Computing (sum)² − product (32).
note: Symmetric functions of roots via Vieta.

text: For how many integer values of m in the range −10 ≤ m ≤ 10 does the equation x² + mx + 9 = 0 have real roots?
solution: Real roots ⇒ m² − 36 ≥ 0 ⇒ |m| ≥ 6.
fast: Count |m| from 6 to 10, doubled.
trap: Using strict inequality and dropping ±6 (gives 8).
note: Real roots ⇔ D ≥ 0 (equal roots included).

text: One root of x² + px + 12 = 0 is 4, and the equation x² + px + q = 0 has equal roots. What is q?
solution: Equal roots ⇒ p² = 4q ⇒ q = 49/4.
fast: Get p from the known root, then D = 0.
hint: Substitute x = 4 in the first equation.
trap: Assuming the second equation also has root 4 (q = 12).
note: Equal roots: q = p²/4.

text: For how many integer values of k with |k| ≤ 12 does the equation x² + kx + 16 = 0 have two distinct negative real roots?
solution: Distinct real roots: k² > 64 ⇒ |k| > 8.
Both negative: sum = −k < 0 ⇒ k > 0; product = 16 > 0 ✓.
fast: Sign of the sum decides the sign of k.
hint: Check discriminant, sum and product of roots.
trap: Counting k = −9 … −12 too (those give positive roots).
note: Both roots negative ⇔ D ≥ 0, sum < 0, product > 0.

text: If the roots of x² − bx + c = 0 are two consecutive integers, what is the value of b² − 4c?
solution: Roots n and n + 1: b = 2n + 1, c = n(n + 1).
fast: b² − 4c = (difference of roots)² = 1.
hint: Discriminant equals the square of the root difference.
trap: Answering 0 (confusing with equal roots).
note: D = (α − β)² for monic quadratics.

text: How many integers n satisfy log₂ n + log₂ (20 − n) > 6?
solution: Domain: 0 < n < 20.
fast: Combine the logs, drop the base, factorise.
hint: Use log a + log b = log ab and check the domain.
trap: Including 4 and 16 (equality, not >) or ignoring the domain.
note: Log inequalities: fix the domain first, then drop the log (base > 1 keeps the sign).

text: If 2^(x+1) + 2^x = 96, what is x?
fast: Factor out the smallest power.
trap: Adding exponents: 2^(2x+1) = 96.
note: aᵐ + aⁿ cannot be combined into one power — factor instead.

text: Given log₁₀ 2 = 0.3010, how many digits does 2⁵⁰ have?
solution: Number of digits = ⌊15.05⌋ + 1 = 16.
fast: Digits = floor(log) + 1.
hint: The characteristic of the log tells the digit count.
trap: Answering 15 (forgetting +1).
note: N has ⌊log₁₀ N⌋ + 1 digits.

solution: Seek a + b = 12, ab = 35 ⇒ a = 7, b = 5.
hint: Find two numbers with sum 12 and product 35.
trap: Picking √10 + √2 (sum 12 but product 20).
note: Nested surd: √(x + 2√y) = √a + √b with a + b = x, ab = y.

text: If log₂ x + log₄ x + log₁₆ x = 7, what is x?
solution: log₄ x = (log₂ x)/2, log₁₆ x = (log₂ x)/4.
fast: Convert all to base 2.
trap: Multiplying instead of dividing by n when changing base.
note: Change of base: log_{a^k} x = (log_a x)/k.

text: What is the sum of all real values of x satisfying 3^(2x) − 10·3^x + 9 = 0?
solution: Let t = 3^x: t² − 10t + 9 = 0 ⇒ t = 1 or 9.
x = 0 or 2 ⇒ sum = 2.
fast: Product of t-roots = 9 = 3^(x₁ + x₂) ⇒ x₁ + x₂ = 2.
trap: Reporting the sum of t-values (10).
note: Exponential quadratics: product of t-roots gives sum of x-roots.

text: For how many integer values of x is |x − 2| + |x + 3| = 5?
solution: |x − 2| + |x + 3| is the sum of distances from x to 2 and to −3.
The two points are 5 apart, so the sum equals 5 exactly when x lies between them: −3 ≤ x ≤ 2.
fast: Sum of distances equals the gap ⇔ x is between the points.
hint: Interpret each modulus as a distance on the number line.
trap: Solving only at the critical points and reporting 2 solutions.
note: |x − a| + |x − b| ≥ |a − b|, with equality on [a, b].

text: A function satisfies f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y) for all real x, y, and f(1) = 3. What is f(5)?
fast: Additive functions on integers are linear: f(n) = n·f(1).
trap: Guessing f(5) = f(1)⁵.
note: Cauchy's equation: f(n) = n f(1) for integers n.

text: What is the minimum value of f(x) = max(2x + 1, 7 − x) over all real x?
solution: The max of an increasing and a decreasing line is smallest where they cross.
fast: Minimum of max(increasing, decreasing) is at their intersection.
trap: Minimising each line separately.
note: min max(…) of opposite-slope lines occurs at intersection.

text: A function f satisfies f(x) + 2f(1 − x) = 3x for all real x. What is f(0)?
fast: Substitute x and 1 − x to get two equations.
trap: Substituting only once and stalling with two unknowns.
note: Functional equations with x and (1 − x): substitute both.

solution: The sum telescopes: ½(1 − 1/21) = ½ × 20/21 = 10/21.
fast: Telescoping: ½(first − last reciprocal).
hint: Split each term into partial fractions.
trap: Forgetting the factor ½ (20/21).

text: What is the sum of all two-digit numbers that are divisible by 7?
fast: n × average of first and last.
trap: Starting from 7 (not two-digit).
note: AP sum = n(first + last)/2.

text: In a geometric progression the 3rd term is 12 and the 6th term is 96. What is the sum of the first five terms?
trap: Using r = 8 (forgetting the cube root).
note: Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹; Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1).

text: The sum of an infinite geometric progression is 20 and its first term is 5. What is its common ratio? (Enter as a decimal.)
trap: Answering 0.25 (that is 1 − r).
note: S∞ exists only for |r| < 1.

text: What is the value of 1·2 + 2·3 + 3·4 + … + 10·11?
fast: Product of three consecutive integers ÷ 3.
trap: Using n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 only (385).

text: The first term of an arithmetic progression is 24, and the sum of its first 10 terms equals the sum of its first 15 terms. What is the common difference?
solution: S₁₀ = S₁₅ ⇒ T₁₁ + … + T₁₅ = 0 ⇒ middle term T₁₃ = 0.
fast: Sₘ = Sₙ ⇒ T at position (m + n + 1)/2 is 0.
hint: Terms 11 to 15 must add up to zero.
trap: Setting T₁₅ = 0 instead of the middle term T₁₃ (gives d = −12/7).
note: Sₘ = Sₙ ⇒ S_(m+n) = 0.

text: What is the remainder when 7¹⁰⁰ is divided by 5?
solution: 7 ≡ 2 (mod 5); powers of 2 mod 5 cycle 2, 4, 3, 1 (length 4).
100 is a multiple of 4 ⇒ remainder 1.
trap: Taking the exponent's remainder as 0 and using 7⁰ incorrectly as 7.
note: Remainder cycles: reduce the base first, then the exponent mod cycle length.

text: How many positive factors does 360 have?
solution: Number of factors = (3 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 24.
fast: Add one to each exponent and multiply.
trap: Multiplying the exponents themselves (3 × 2 × 1 = 6).

text: How many natural numbers less than 1000 leave a remainder of 3 when divided by 5 and a remainder of 4 when divided by 7?
fast: Find the smallest solution by scanning the larger modulus's list, then step by the LCM.
hint: Find the first number satisfying both, then add 35 repeatedly.
trap: Off-by-one: forgetting the '+1' in the AP count (28).
note: Two remainder conditions ⇒ solutions form an AP with difference = LCM.

text: How many trailing zeros does 100! have?
fast: Keep dividing by 5 and add the quotients.
hint: Zeros come from 2 × 5 pairs; 5s are scarcer.
trap: Forgetting the extra 5s from 25, 50, 75, 100 (answering 20).
note: Trailing zeros of n! = Σ⌊n/5ᵏ⌋.

text: What is the remainder when 17²³ + 23²³ is divided by 40?
solution: For odd n, aⁿ + bⁿ is divisible by (a + b).
17 + 23 = 40 and 23 is odd ⇒ 17²³ + 23²³ is a multiple of 40.
Remainder = 0.
fast: Spot a + b = divisor with an odd exponent.
trap: Computing each remainder separately and adding wrongly, or using the rule for even n (aⁿ − bⁿ).
note: Odd n: (a + b) | aⁿ + bⁿ. Any n: (a − b) | aⁿ − bⁿ.

text: What is the smallest natural number that leaves remainders 1, 2 and 3 when divided by 2, 3 and 4 respectively?
solution: In each case the remainder is one less than the divisor, so N + 1 is divisible by 2, 3 and 4.
fast: Constant 'deficit' (divisor − remainder = 1) ⇒ N = LCM − 1.
trap: Answering the LCM itself (12).
note: Common deficit d ⇒ N = k·LCM − d.

text: What is the sum of all positive factors of 72?
fast: Multiply the sums of prime-power series.
trap: Excluding 1 or 72 from the sum.

text: What is the units digit of 3⁶⁵ × 7⁴⁹?
solution: Units digits of 3ⁿ and 7ⁿ cycle with length 4.
65 ≡ 1 (mod 4) ⇒ 3⁶⁵ ends in 3; 49 ≡ 1 (mod 4) ⇒ 7⁴⁹ ends in 7.
3 × 7 = 21 ⇒ units digit 1.
fast: Reduce exponents mod 4.
hint: Units digits of powers repeat every 4.
trap: Using exponent mod 2 or adding the digits instead of multiplying.
note: Cyclicity 4 for 2, 3, 7, 8; 2 for 4, 9; 1 for 0, 1, 5, 6.

text: The HCF of two numbers is 27 and their LCM is 2079. If one of the numbers lies between 250 and 500, what is the other number?
solution: Write the numbers as 27a and 27b with a, b co-prime and ab = 2079/27 = 77.
Co-prime pairs: (1, 77) or (7, 11).
(1, 77) gives 27 and 2079 — neither in 250–500. (7, 11) gives 189 and 297.
297 lies in the range ⇒ the other number is 189.
fast: LCM/HCF = 77 = 7 × 11 ⇒ numbers are 27 × 7 and 27 × 11.
hint: Divide the LCM by the HCF and split the result into co-prime factors.
trap: Choosing 297 — that is the number in the range, not the other one.
note: Numbers = H·a, H·b with gcd(a, b) = 1 and ab = L/H.

text: How many integers from 1 to 1000 (inclusive) are divisible by neither 3 nor 5?
solution: Divisible by 3: 333; by 5: 200; by 15: 66.
Divisible by 3 or 5 = 333 + 200 − 66 = 467.
fast: Inclusion–exclusion with floors.
trap: Forgetting to add back the 66 multiples of 15, which gives 467.

text: In triangle ABC, AB = 10 cm, AC = 17 cm and BC = 21 cm. What is the length (in cm) of the altitude from A to BC?
solution: Altitude = 2 × 84/21 = 8.
fast: Alternatively split BC as x + (21 − x): 10² − x² = 17² − (21 − x)² ⇒ x = 6, h = 8.
hint: Find the area with Heron's formula, then use ½ × base × height.
trap: Dividing the area by 21 without doubling (4).
note: h = 2Δ/base. Triangles 10-17-21 and 13-14-15 both have area 84.

text: In triangle ABC, D lies on AB and E on AC such that DE ∥ BC and AD : DB = 2 : 3. If the area of triangle ABC is 100 cm², what is the area (in cm²) of trapezium DBCE?
solution: AD/AB = 2/5 ⇒ area(ADE)/area(ABC) = 4/25.
area(ADE) = 16 ⇒ trapezium = 100 − 16 = 84.
fast: Area ratio = (side ratio)².
trap: Using 2/3 as the similarity ratio (AD/DB instead of AD/AB).
note: Similar figures: areas scale as the square of lengths.

text: Two circles of radii 5 cm and 3 cm touch each other externally. What is the length of a direct (external) common tangent?
options: 4√3 cm
8 cm
solution: Distance between centres d = 5 + 3 = 8.
Direct common tangent = √(d² − (r₁ − r₂)²) = √(64 − 4) = √60 = 2√15 cm.
fast: For circles touching externally, direct tangent = 2√(r₁r₂) = 2√15.
hint: Draw the tangent and shift it to pass through the smaller centre.
trap: Using (r₁ + r₂)² — that is for the transverse tangent (which is 0 here).
note: Direct: √(d² − (r₁ − r₂)²); transverse: √(d² − (r₁ + r₂)²).

text: A convex polygon has 54 diagonals. Each of its interior angles is equal. What is the measure (in degrees) of each interior angle?
solution: Exterior angle = 360/12 = 30° ⇒ interior = 150°.
trap: Using n(n − 1)/2 (that counts sides too).
note: Interior angle of a regular n-gon = 180 − 360/n.

text: From a point P that is 13 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm, a tangent is drawn. What is the length of the tangent?
options: 8 cm
18 cm
12 cm
solution: Radius ⟂ tangent at the point of contact.
Tangent = √(13² − 5²) = 12 cm.
fast: 5-12-13 triplet.
hint: The radius meets the tangent at 90°.
trap: Adding instead of subtracting squares.
note: Tangent length from P = √(d² − r²).

text: What is the inradius of a triangle with sides 13, 14 and 15 units?
fast: Memorise: the 13-14-15 triangle has area 84.
trap: Dividing area by the full perimeter (2).
note: Inradius r = Δ/s; circumradius R = abc/4Δ.

text: An equilateral triangle is inscribed in a circle of radius 6 cm. What is the square of the side of the triangle (in cm²)?
solution: For an equilateral triangle, R = a/√3 ⇒ a = 6√3.
hint: Circumradius of an equilateral triangle is a/√3.
trap: Using the inradius formula a/(2√3) (a = 12√3).
note: Equilateral: R = a/√3, r = a/(2√3), R = 2r.

text: How many points with integer coordinates lie strictly inside the triangle formed by the lines x = 0, y = 0 and x + y = 10?
solution: Strictly inside ⇒ x ≥ 1, y ≥ 1, x + y ≤ 9.
For x = 1 … 8, y can take 9 − x values: 8 + 7 + … + 1 = 36.
fast: Substitute x = a + 1, y = b + 1: a + b ≤ 7 ⇒ C(9, 2) = 36.
hint: Fix x and count the allowed y values.
trap: Including boundary points on x + y = 10 (gives 45).
note: Interior lattice points of the triangle x, y > 0, x + y < n: (n − 1)(n − 2)/2.

text: What is the area (in square units) of the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (8, 0) and (3, 6)?
solution: Base along the x-axis = 8; height = y-coordinate of the third vertex = 6.
fast: When one side lies on an axis, use base × height directly.
hint: Look for a side on an axis.
trap: Using the slanted side as the base.
note: Shoelace: ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|.

text: The diagonals of a rhombus are 16 cm and 12 cm. What is its perimeter?
options: 40 cm
48 cm
56 cm
28 cm
solution: Diagonals bisect at right angles: half-diagonals 8 and 6 ⇒ side = 10.
Perimeter = 40 cm.
fast: 6-8-10 triplet again.
hint: Diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular bisectors.
trap: Using full diagonals as legs (side 20).
note: Rhombus side = ½√(d₁² + d₂²).

text: An arc of a circle subtends an angle of 110° at the centre. What angle does it subtend at a point on the remaining (major) arc of the circle?
solution: Inscribed angle = half the central angle on the same arc = 55°.
fast: Halve the central angle.
hint: Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference.
trap: Answering 125° (the angle from a point on the minor arc).
note: Point on the minor arc sees 180° − 55° = 125°.

text: The total surface area of a cube is 150 cm². What is its volume?
options: 150 cm³
216 cm³
100 cm³
125 cm³
solution: 6a² = 150 ⇒ a = 5 ⇒ volume = 125 cm³.
fast: Divide by 6, take the square root, cube it.
trap: Using 4 faces (lateral area).
note: Cube: TSA 6a², volume a³, diagonal a√3.

text: What is the volume (in cm³) of a cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm? (Take π = 22/7.)
trap: Using 2πrh (curved surface area, 440).
note: Cylinder CSA 2πrh, TSA 2πr(r + h).

text: A solid metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into solid cones of base radius 3 cm and height 4 cm. How many cones are formed?
solution: Sphere volume = (4/3)π × 216 = 288π.
Cone volume = (1/3)π × 9 × 4 = 12π.
fast: Cancel π and 1/3 first: (4 × 216)/(9 × 4) = 24.
trap: Comparing surface areas.
note: Recasting problems: equate volumes.

text: In how many distinct arrangements of the letters of BANANA are no two A's adjacent?
solution: Arrange B, N, N first: 3!/2! = 3 ways.
This creates 4 gaps (_ B _ N _ N _); choose 3 of them for the identical A's: C(4, 3) = 4.
fast: Gap method: arrange the others, then drop the restricted letters into gaps.
trap: Using total − (all A's together) = 60 − 4 = 56, which still allows two A's to be adjacent.
note: No two X adjacent ⇒ arrange the rest, choose gaps for X.

text: In how many ways can a committee of 3 men and 2 women be chosen from 6 men and 5 women?
fast: Independent choices multiply.
trap: Adding the two counts (30).
note: AND ⇒ multiply; OR ⇒ add.

text: Three different numbers are chosen at random from 1, 2, …, 10. What is the probability that they can be arranged to form an arithmetic progression?
solution: Total selections = C(10, 3) = 120.
AP triples {a, a + d, a + 2d} ≤ 10: d = 1 → 8, d = 2 → 6, d = 3 → 4, d = 4 → 2. Total 20.
Probability = 20/120 = 1/6.
fast: Equivalently, count pairs (first, last) of the same parity: the middle is fixed. Odd pairs C(5,2) + even pairs C(5,2) = 20.
hint: The middle term is the average of the other two.
trap: Counting ordered triples in the numerator but unordered in the denominator.
note: a, b, c in AP ⇔ a + c = 2b ⇔ a and c have the same parity.

text: In how many ways can 10 identical chocolates be distributed among 3 children so that each child gets at least 2?
solution: Give 2 to each first; 4 remain to be distributed freely.
Non-negative solutions of a + b + c = 4: C(6, 2) = 15.
fast: Pre-allocate the minimum, then stars and bars.
hint: Hand out the compulsory 2 each first.
trap: Using C(9, 2) = 36 (at least 1 each).

text: A bag contains 5 red and 4 blue balls. Three balls are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that exactly two of them are red?
fast: Hypergeometric: choose reds and blues separately.
trap: Mixing ordered numerator with unordered denominator.
note: P = C(R, r)C(B, b)/C(R + B, r + b).

text: Who sits in seat 4?
options: Farhan
Bela
Divya
Chirag
solution: Clue 5 puts Arun in seat 2, 4 or 6; clue 2 puts Farhan three seats away, and clue 6 keeps Farhan off the ends.
Testing Esha at seat 7 (clue 1) with Arun at 6 forces Farhan to 3; Divya–Bela then need two adjacent free seats to the right of Farhan: seats 4–5.
Gopal must be left of Farhan (clue 7) and Chirag off the ends (clue 8) ⇒ Gopal 1, Chirag 2.
Final order (1→7): Gopal, Chirag, Farhan, Divya, Bela, Arun, Esha. Every other placement of Esha/Arun breaks a clue.
Seat 4: Divya.
fast: Start from the most restrictive pair (Arun–Farhan with a gap of 2 and Arun in an even seat), then place the Divya–Bela block.
hint: Fix Esha at an end, then try the three possible seats for Arun.
trap: Treating 'exactly two people between' as a gap of 2 seats instead of 3.
note: Blocks (like Divya–Bela) and fixed gaps are the anchors in linear arrangements.

text: How many people sit between Chirag and Bela?
solution: Chirag is in seat 2 and Bela in seat 5.
Seats 3 and 4 lie between them ⇒ 2 people.
fast: People between = |difference of seats| − 1.
trap: Reporting the seat difference (3).
note: Between-count = gap − 1.

text: Who sits immediately to the left of Arun?
options: Divya
Bela
Farhan
Esha
solution: Arun is in seat 6; the person in seat 5 is Bela.
fast: Left = one seat lower.
trap: Reading 'left' as the higher seat number.
note: Define directions before solving; the set text does it for you.

text: If clue 7 (Gopal sits somewhere to the left of Farhan) is dropped, how many different seating arrangements satisfy all the remaining clues?
solution: Without clue 7, the valid orders are:
G C F D B A E, D B F C G A E, D B F G C A E, E C F D B A G (and C G F D B A E, which clue 8 removes because Chirag is at an end).
Count = 4.
fast: List the cases systematically by Esha's end and Arun's seat.
hint: Keep clue 8 in force while counting.
trap: Forgetting clue 8 and counting 5.
note: 'If a clue is removed' questions: recount every case, don't just flip one.

text: Who sits exactly midway between Farhan and Esha?
options: Bela
Gopal
Arun
Divya
solution: Farhan is in seat 3, Esha in seat 7 ⇒ midpoint seat 5 = Bela.
fast: Midpoint seat = average of the two seat numbers.
trap: Choosing Divya (seat 4), which is nearer to Farhan.
note: Midway exists only when the seat numbers have the same parity.

text: Who sits directly opposite Kavya?
options: Sana
Omkar
Nikhil
Rohan
solution: Number seats clockwise from Kavya (0). Clue 1: Priya = 2. Clue 7: Omkar = 3. Clue 2: Rohan = 6.
Clue 6: Leela is next to Priya and seat 3 is taken ⇒ Leela = 1.
Clue 3: Manav is at 5 or 7. If Manav = 5, Nikhil (clue 5, three seats anticlockwise) = 2 — taken. So Manav = 7 and Nikhil = 4.
Sana takes the last seat, 5 (not adjacent to Kavya ✓).
Clockwise from Kavya: Kavya, Leela, Priya, Omkar, Nikhil, Sana, Rohan, Manav.
Opposite Kavya (seat 4): Nikhil.
fast: Fix Kavya at 0 and convert every clue into a seat offset.
hint: Priya's seat follows directly from clue 1.
trap: Mixing up the left/right convention for people facing the centre.
note: Circular: fix one person to remove rotations; facing centre ⇒ left = clockwise.

text: Who sits second to the right of Sana?
options: Omkar
Priya
Nikhil
Manav
solution: Sana is at seat 5. Second to the right = two seats anticlockwise = seat 3 = Omkar.
fast: Right = anticlockwise = subtract.
hint: Count two seats anticlockwise from Sana.
trap: Counting clockwise (gives Manav).
note: Write the direction convention next to your diagram.

text: Counting in the clockwise direction from Leela, how many people sit between Leela and Rohan?
solution: Leela = 1, Rohan = 6. Clockwise between them: seats 2, 3, 4, 5 ⇒ 4 people.
fast: Clockwise gap − 1.
trap: Counting anticlockwise (2 people: Kavya, Manav).
note: In circles always state the direction of counting.

text: Which of the following pairs are immediate neighbours?
options: Priya and Sana
Rohan and Nikhil
Manav and Kavya
Leela and Omkar
solution: Manav (7) and Kavya (0) are adjacent. Leela–Omkar (1, 3), Priya–Sana (2, 5) and Rohan–Nikhil (6, 4) are not.
fast: Seats 7 and 0 are adjacent in a circle.
trap: Forgetting that the last and first seats touch.
note: Adjacency in circles is modulo n.

text: If Kavya and Sana exchange seats (everyone else stays put), who will sit immediately to the left of Kavya?
options: Manav
Rohan
Nikhil
Sana
solution: After the swap Kavya is at seat 5. Immediate left = next seat clockwise = 6 = Rohan.
fast: Only the two swapped seats change; read the neighbour directly.
hint: Kavya moves to Sana's old seat.
trap: Answering Nikhil (that is Kavya's right after the swap).
note: After swaps, recompute only the affected positions.

text: Which lecture is held on Tuesday morning?
options: Strategy
HR
Marketing
Finance
solution: Clues 3 and 4: Tech (morning) and Operations (afternoon) share one day.
Clue 1 with clue 5: Marketing is on Tuesday and Strategy on Wednesday.
So Tech–Operations is on Monday.
HR is a morning lecture (6) and Finance an afternoon one (7), on different days (2); Finance is not with Strategy (8) ⇒ Finance is on Tuesday afternoon, so Marketing is Tuesday morning.
HR then takes Wednesday morning and Strategy Wednesday afternoon.
Schedule: Mon – Tech, Operations; Tue – Marketing, Finance; Wed – HR, Strategy.
fast: Pair up linked lectures (Tech→Operations) first; they occupy a whole day.
hint: Tech and Operations must be on the same day.
trap: Placing Operations on the next day's morning; 'immediately after' stays within the same day because Tech is in the morning.
note: Block the tightest pair first, then use day-level clues.

text: Which lecture is held immediately before Strategy?
options: Finance
Operations
Marketing
HR
solution: Strategy is Wednesday afternoon; Wednesday morning is HR.
fast: Read off the schedule.
trap: Choosing Finance (last slot of the previous day, not immediately before).
note: 'Immediately before' = previous slot.

text: How many lectures are held between Tech and HR?
solution: Tech = slot 1 (Mon AM), HR = slot 5 (Wed AM). Between: Operations, Marketing, Finance ⇒ 3.
fast: Slot gap − 1.
trap: Counting the day gap (2) instead of slots.
note: Linearise multi-day schedules into numbered slots.

text: If clue 5 (Marketing is not held on Monday) is removed, how many different schedules satisfy the remaining clues?
solution: Without clue 5 the Tech–Operations block can sit on any day, and Marketing may be on Monday.
Place the block, then Marketing (earlier day than Strategy), then HR (morning) and Finance (afternoon) on different days, keeping Finance away from Strategy.
Valid schedules:
(i) Mon: Tech, Operations | Tue: Marketing, Finance | Wed: HR, Strategy
(ii) Mon: Marketing, Finance | Tue: Tech, Operations | Wed: HR, Strategy
(iii) Mon: Marketing, Finance | Tue: HR, Strategy | Wed: Tech, Operations
Count = 3.
fast: Enumerate by the day of the Tech–Operations block (3 choices) and fill the rest.
trap: Stopping at the first alternative found.
note: Clue-removal questions need a full re-enumeration.

text: Which lecture is held on the same day as Finance?
options: Strategy
HR
Operations
Marketing
solution: Finance is Tuesday afternoon; Tuesday morning is Marketing.
fast: Read off the schedule.
trap: Choosing Strategy (clue 8 forbids it).
note: Double-check answers against the 'different day' clues.

text: What is the minimum number of days needed to complete the whole project?
solution: Earliest finish (EF) = max EF of prerequisites + duration.
Project length = 16 days.
fast: Forward pass: carry the latest prerequisite finish.
hint: Compute each task's earliest finish in dependency order.
trap: Adding all durations (29) — tasks run in parallel.
note: Project length = longest path through the dependency network.

text: What is the earliest time by which task E can be completed?
solution: E needs C, which needs A: 3 + 4 + 2 = 9.
fast: Follow the chain A → C → E.
hint: E's only chain is A, C, E.
trap: Including D (not a prerequisite of E).
note: Earliest finish depends only on the task's own ancestors.

text: By how many days can task G be delayed (beyond its earliest finish) without delaying the project?
solution: G's earliest finish = 9. H must start by 16 − 2 = 14, so G's latest finish = 14.
Slack = 14 − 9 = 5 days.
fast: Slack = latest finish − earliest finish.
hint: Work backwards from the project end to find G's latest finish.
trap: Comparing with F's finish (14) and forgetting H's duration, or comparing with E.
note: Backward pass: LF = min(LS of successors).

text: If task D takes 8 days instead of 6, what is the new minimum project duration?
options: 16 days
18 days
17 days
19 days
solution: D: 5 → 13, F: 13 → 16, H: 16 → 18. New duration = 18 days.
fast: D is on the critical path, so the whole delay passes through.
trap: Assuming slack absorbs the delay (answering 16).
note: Delays on critical tasks add one-for-one to the project length.

text: Which tasks lie on the critical path?
options: A, C, E, F, H
A, D, F, H
B, G, H
B, D, F, H
solution: Tasks with zero slack: B (0–5), D (5–11), F (11–14), H (14–16).
A, C, E and G all have slack.
fast: Trace back from H through the prerequisite that finished last.
hint: Follow the 'binding' prerequisite at each step.
trap: Choosing A → C → E → F → H (that path totals only 14).
note: Critical path = chain of zero-slack tasks.

text: How many chocolates does Charu get?
solution: Ekta has the fewest, so Ekta = 1 is the natural start; Bhanu ≥ 2 so Asha ≥ 4.
Try Bhanu = 2, Asha = 4: Charu + Dev = 13 with Dev > 2 and Charu > Dev + 1. Charu a multiple of 4 ⇒ Charu = 8, Dev = 5 ✓ (8 > 6).
Bhanu = 3, Asha = 6: Charu + Dev = 10, Dev ≥ 4, Charu > Dev + 1 ⇒ Charu = 8 needs Dev = 2 ✗.
Larger Bhanu leaves too few chocolates. Ekta ≥ 2 also fails.
Unique: Asha 4, Bhanu 2, Charu 8, Dev 5, Ekta 1.
fast: Drive the case split by Bhanu's value; Asha follows automatically.
trap: Forgetting that all five numbers must be different.
note: Distribution sets: case on the most constrained variable.

text: Who gets the second-highest number of chocolates?
options: Charu
Asha
Dev
Bhanu
solution: Order: Charu 8, Dev 5, Asha 4, Bhanu 2, Ekta 1 ⇒ Dev.
fast: Sort the final distribution.
trap: Picking Asha (third).
note: Rank questions: write the sorted list once.

text: What is the difference between the numbers of chocolates Dev and Bhanu get?
solution: Dev 5 − Bhanu 2 = 3.
fast: Direct subtraction.
trap: Using Asha instead of Bhanu (1).
note: Read names carefully in similar-looking options.

text: If clue 5 (Charu's number is a multiple of 4) is removed, how many distributions satisfy the remaining clues?
solution: Without clue 5 the valid distributions are:
Asha 4, Bhanu 2, Charu 8, Dev 5, Ekta 1 and Asha 4, Bhanu 2, Charu 10, Dev 3, Ekta 1.
Count = 2.
fast: Re-run the Bhanu = 2 case without the multiple-of-4 filter.
hint: Only the Bhanu = 2 case survives the other clues.
trap: Forgetting that Dev must exceed Bhanu, which would admit extra cases.
note: Each clue usually kills specific cases; note which.

text: Suppose that after the distribution Charu gives 3 of her chocolates to Ekta. Who then has the largest number of chocolates?
options: Charu only
Asha and Ekta (tied)
Dev only
Charu and Dev (tied)
solution: New counts: Charu 5, Ekta 4, Asha 4, Bhanu 2, Dev 5.
Charu and Dev tie at 5.
fast: Update just the two changed values.
trap: Answering 'Charu only' without checking Dev.
note: After transfers, check for ties.

text: How many different task forces can be formed?
solution: (Initials: A = Aarav, B = Bhavya, F = Farah, G = Gautam, H = Hina.)
Exactly one doctor ⇒ four places for engineers and lawyers, with ≥ 2 engineers and ≥ 1 lawyer.
Case 1 — Chitra and Dhruv both in: pick two more from {A, B, F, G, H} with at least one lawyer.
· With Jaya: {A,G}, {A,H}, {B,G}, {F,G}, {F,H}, {G,H} are valid; {A,F} breaks clue 2; {B,F} and {B,H} break clue 3 ⇒ 6.
· With Ishaan (Gautam barred by clue 6): {A,H}, {F,H} ⇒ 2.
Case 2 — Chitra and Dhruv both out: the engineers must be Aarav and Bhavya ⇒ Gautam is in (clue 3), Farah is out (clue 2), so the fourth place is Hina; the doctor must be Jaya (clue 6) ⇒ 1.
fast: Split on the Chitra–Dhruv pair (in or out); it forces most of the structure.
hint: Start with the 'both or neither' pair.
trap: Missing the Chitra–Dhruv-out case, or forgetting that clue 6 removes Gautam when Ishaan is chosen.
note: Selection sets: branch on the 'both-or-neither' and 'if-then' clues.

text: If Hina is not selected, how many task forces are possible?
solution: From the 9 teams, those without Hina: {A,C,D,G,J}, {B,C,D,G,J}, {C,D,F,G,J} ⇒ 3.
fast: Filter the full list.
trap: Counting teams without Farah instead.
note: Keep the full list of cases written out — later questions reuse it.

text: If Bhavya is selected, how many task forces are possible?
solution: Teams containing Bhavya: {A,B,G,H,J} and {B,C,D,G,J} ⇒ 2.
fast: Bhavya forces Gautam, which forces Jaya.
trap: Allowing Ishaan with Gautam.
note: Chained conditionals shrink the space fast.

text: If Ishaan is selected, which of the following must be true?
options: Farah is selected
Gautam is selected
Aarav is selected
Hina is selected
solution: Teams with Ishaan: {A,C,D,H,I} and {C,D,F,H,I}. Both include Hina.
fast: Ishaan bars Gautam, so the lawyer must be Hina (with or without Farah).
hint: Which lawyers remain once Gautam is out?
trap: Choosing Aarav (true in only one of the two teams).
note: 'Must be true' = true in every surviving case.

text: What is the maximum number of lawyers that can be on the task force?
solution: Engineers ≥ 2 and one doctor leave at most 2 places for lawyers; e.g. {C, D, G, H, J}. So 2.
fast: 5 − 2 engineers − 1 doctor = 2.
trap: Answering 3 (all lawyers) without checking the minimums.
note: Max/min questions: fill the compulsory seats first.

text: How many matches in the league ended in a draw?
solution: 10 matches were played. Each decisive match gives 3 points in total, each draw 2.
Total points = 28 = 3 × 10 − (number of draws) ⇒ draws = 2.
fast: Total-points identity: 3M − D = total.
hint: Add up all the points first.
trap: Assuming every team with a non-multiple of 3 drew separately (counting 4).
note: Win/draw/loss leagues: total = 3 × matches − draws.

text: What was the result of the match between P and Q?
options: Cannot be determined
P won
Draw
Q won
solution: T has 1 point ⇒ one draw (vs S) and three losses; S–T is one of the two draws.
P has 10 = 3 wins + 1 draw. Q has 7 = 2 wins + 1 draw. R has 6 = 2 wins and no draw. S has 4 = 1 win + 1 draw (the draw is with T).
So the second draw involves both P and Q ⇒ P drew with Q.
fast: Decompose each total into wins and draws: 10 = 3+3+3+1, 7 = 3+3+1, 6 = 3+3, 4 = 3+1, 1 = 1.
hint: Who needs a draw, and who already has one?
trap: Pairing P's draw with T (ruled out by the given clue).
note: Points decomposition is the key step in league puzzles.

text: How many matches did R win?
solution: R has 6 points and no draws are available for R (both draws are P–Q and S–T) ⇒ 2 wins.
hint: Could R have drawn any match?
trap: Answering 6 (points, not wins).
note: Always separate points from wins.

text: If it is also known that Q beat R, what was the result of the match between R and S?
options: Draw
R won
S won
Cannot be determined
solution: Q's two wins: over T and, now, R. So Q lost to S.
S's single win is therefore over Q, so S lost to R ⇒ R won.
fast: Track each team's remaining wins as a budget.
hint: S has exactly one win; whom did it beat?
trap: Assuming S beat R because S beat Q earlier in the case list.
note: In league problems, win budgets propagate quickly.

text: How many different sets of match results are consistent with all the given information?
solution: Fixed: P beat R, S, T; P drew Q; Q and R beat T; S drew T.
Remaining: Q–R, Q–S, R–S with Q needing 1 more win, R 1 more, S 1 win.
These form a cycle: either Q>R, R>S, S>Q or R>Q, S>R, Q>S ⇒ 2 sets.
fast: After fixing forced results, the leftover three matches form a win cycle.
trap: Counting the 4 sets possible without the 'T's point' clue.
note: Count possibilities only after applying every clue.

text: Which seed won the tournament?
solution: Clue 4: 8 beat 1 (upset 1). Clue 2: 5 reached the final, so 5 beat 4 (upset 2) and then beat 8 in semi-final 1 (not an upset).
Clue 6: 3 beat 6. Clue 5: 2 beat 7.
Semi-final 2 is 3 vs 2. The final is 5 vs the winner; clue 3 says the champion is not 5.
Exactly one more upset is needed (clue 1). If 2 beat 3 there is no upset in SF2; then the final (5 vs 2, won by 2) is not an upset ⇒ total 2 ✗.
So 3 beat 2 (upset 3), and 3 beat 5 in the final (not an upset) ⇒ champion = seed 3.
fast: Count upsets as you go; the last one decides SF2.
hint: Work round by round; list which matches are forced.
trap: Calling 5-beats-8 an upset (5 is the stronger seed there).
note: Upset bookkeeping: compare seed numbers in every match.

text: Whom did seed 5 beat in the semi-final?
options: Seed 3
Seed 8
Seed 4
Seed 1
solution: Semi-final 1 was 8 (who beat 1) vs 5 ⇒ seed 8.
fast: Seed 1 was already out.
trap: Answering seed 1 without applying clue 4.
note: Track the bracket path explicitly.

text: How many matches did seed 2 win?
solution: 2 beat 7 in round 1 and lost to 3 in the semi-final ⇒ 1 win.
fast: Read from the bracket.
trap: Assuming seed 2 reached the final.
note: Wins in a knockout = rounds survived.

text: If clue 6 is removed, how many different tournament outcomes are possible?
solution: Without clue 6, SF2 can be 3 vs 2 (as before) or 6 vs 2.
6 vs 2 case: 6 beat 3 (upset 3), so 2 must beat 6 in SF2 (no more upsets) and 2 beats 5 in the final ✓ (champion 2 < 5).
Together with the original outcome ⇒ 2 outcomes.
fast: Only the 3 vs 6 result is released; recount upsets.
trap: Letting 6 also win the semi-final (that makes 4 upsets).
note: Removing a clue reopens only the matches it fixed.

text: Which of the following matches was an upset?
options: Seed 5 vs seed 8 (semi-final)
Seed 3 vs seed 2 (semi-final)
Seed 2 vs seed 7 (first round)
Seed 3 vs seed 5 (final)
solution: Upsets: 8 over 1, 5 over 4, 3 over 2. Among the options, only seed 3 vs seed 2 (semi-final) was an upset.
fast: The weaker seed (higher number) won.
trap: Treating the final (3 beat 5) as an upset.
note: Define 'upset' once and apply it mechanically.

text: What is the minimum time (in minutes) to travel from A to F?
solution: Shortest times from A: C = 2, B = 3 (via C), D = 8 (A–C–B–D), E = 10 (via C directly or via D), F = 13 (E + 3).
D–F gives 8 + 6 = 14, which is longer.
fast: Label each town with its best time from A, nearest first (Dijkstra by hand).
hint: Go to C first; A–B directly is slower than A–C–B.
trap: Taking A–B (4) directly and missing the 3-minute route via C.
note: Label towns in order of distance; never revisit a finalised town.

text: If road B–D is closed, what is the minimum time (in minutes) from A to F?
solution: A–C–E–F = 2 + 8 + 3 = 13 does not use B–D, so the minimum is unchanged at 13.
fast: Check whether an alternative shortest route avoids the closed road.
hint: There are two shortest routes to F.
trap: Assuming any closure on a shortest path must increase the time.
note: A closure matters only if every shortest route uses that road.

text: How many different routes from A to F take the minimum possible time?
solution: Routes of 13 minutes: A–C–B–D–E–F (2+1+5+2+3) and A–C–E–F (2+8+3) ⇒ 2.
fast: Count ties while labelling: E is reached in 10 two ways.
trap: Counting A–B–D–E–F (14 minutes).
note: Number of shortest paths = sum over tied predecessors.

text: A courier must go from A to F and must pass through D on the way. What is the minimum time (in minutes)?
solution: A to D minimum = 8 (A–C–B–D). D to F minimum = 5 (D–E–F).
Total = 13.
fast: Split into A→D and D→F and minimise each.
hint: Via-point routes: shortest(A, D) + shortest(D, F).
trap: Using the direct D–F road (6) and getting 14.
note: Forced waypoint: add two shortest distances.

text: If road E–F is closed for repairs, what is the minimum time from A to F?
options: 13 minutes
15 minutes
16 minutes
14 minutes
solution: The only other road into F is D–F (6). Minimum A to D = 8.
Minimum = 8 + 6 = 14 minutes.
fast: Identify the roads entering F.
hint: With E–F gone, F can only be reached from D.
trap: Going A–C–E–D–F (2 + 8 + 2 + 6 = 18) without checking the D route.
note: When the last link is cut, work backwards from the destination.

text: What is the maximum flow (in MLD) that can reach T?
solution: Only two pipes enter T: C→T (8) and D→T (7), so flow ≤ 15.
C receives only from A→C (6) ⇒ C→T carries at most 6.
D→T carries at most 7 (enough water reaches D via S→B→D).
Maximum = 6 + 7 = 13, achieved e.g. by S→A→C→T (6), S→B→D→T (7).
The cut {A→C, D→T} has capacity 13, confirming the maximum.
fast: Look for a small set of pipes whose removal disconnects S from T (min cut = max flow).
hint: Check what can actually reach C and D.
trap: Answering 15 (sum of the two pipes into T) without checking what feeds C.
note: Max-flow = min-cut: find the cheapest set of pipes separating S and T.

text: If the capacity of pipe D→T is increased from 7 to 10 MLD, what is the new maximum flow?
solution: Now D→T can take 10: feeds to D are B→D (9) plus A→D (4) and C→D (2), plenty.
Max flow = 6 (via C) + 10 (via D) = 16. New min cut {A→C, D→T} = 16.
fast: Recheck the min cut with the new capacity.
trap: Adding 3 to 13 without checking other cuts (it happens to work here, but verify).
note: After a capacity change, re-evaluate every candidate cut.

text: Which one pipe, if its capacity were increased by 5 MLD, would increase the maximum flow the most?
options: A→C
B→D
D→T
S→A
solution: Only pipes in the minimum cut {A→C, D→T} can help.
A→C +5: C→T limit 8 ⇒ flow via C rises to 8 ⇒ total 15.
D→T +5: D can receive up to 9 + 4 + 2 = 15 ≥ 12 ⇒ total 6 + 12 = 18.
S→A and B→D are not bottlenecks (no gain). Best: D→T.
fast: Only min-cut pipes can raise the max flow.
hint: Which pipes are saturated in every maximum flow?
trap: Choosing A→C without noticing C→T caps it at 8.
note: Upgrade the bottleneck whose downstream has spare capacity.

text: If pipe A→C is shut down completely, what is the maximum flow (in MLD) to T?
solution: C now receives nothing, so C→T carries 0. All flow must use D→T (7).
Maximum = 7.
fast: With A→C gone, C is a dead end.
trap: Routing via C→D→T without realising D→T is already the limit.
note: Removing a pipe can isolate a whole branch.

text: If a new pipe B→C with capacity 4 MLD is added (all else unchanged), what is the new maximum flow?
solution: C can now receive 6 (A→C) + 4 (B→C) = 10, but C→T is limited to 8.
D→T still carries 7. Supply: S→A 10, S→B 8 — enough (e.g. S→A→C 6, S→B→C 2, S→B→D 6, S→A→D 1).
Max flow = 8 + 7 = 15.
fast: New bottlenecks: C→T (8) and D→T (7).
trap: Adding the full 4 to 13 (17), ignoring C→T's cap.
note: Adding capacity helps only up to the next bottleneck.

text: How many units of W were sold in Q4?
solution: W: Q1 = 40, Q2 = 45 ⇒ constant increase of 5 (clue 1) ⇒ Q3 = 50, Q4 = 55.
fast: Constant increments ⇒ arithmetic progression.
hint: Use clue 1 with Q1 and Q2.
trap: Using the total to split the remainder equally (52.5 each).
note: Always verify filled values against the row total.

text: In which quarter were the combined sales of all four products the highest?
options: Q3
Q4
Q2
Q1
solution: Column totals: Q1 145, Q2 150, Q3 155, Q4 170 ⇒ Q4.
fast: Column totals are given directly.
trap: Filling cells before checking whether the given totals already answer the question.
note: Check whether a question needs the missing cells at all.

text: Which product had the highest percentage increase in sales from Q1 to Q4?
options: Y
X
W
Z
hint: You need Y's Q1 and Z's Q4.
trap: Comparing absolute increases (W +15, Y +20 still gives Y, but X/W comparisons often flip).
note: Percentage change: always divide by the base value.

text: In how many quarters did X sell more units than Y?
fast: Compare the two completed rows.
hint: Fill X Q2, X Q4 and Y Q1 first.
trap: Counting ties or reversing the comparison.
note: Pairwise row comparisons are quick once the table is complete.

text: The company earns ₹200 per unit of W, ₹300 per unit of X, ₹250 per unit of Y and ₹150 per unit of Z. Which product earned the highest annual revenue?
options: W
Z
X
Y
fast: Use row totals × price.
trap: Picking W or Z for having the most units.
note: Revenue = volume × price; high volume ≠ high revenue.

text: Who has the highest final score?
options: Cyrus
Bala
Dia
Anu
solution: Final scores: Anu 7+8+8 = 23; Bala 7+8+9 = 24; Cyrus 7+8+8 = 23; Dia 7+9+9 = 25; Ehsan 7+8+8 = 23.
Highest: Dia (25).
fast: Sum of all five − max − min.
hint: Drop exactly one max and one min.
trap: Dropping both 9s for Bala (duplicates) — only one copy is dropped.
note: Trimmed sum = total − max − min.

text: How many finalists share the lowest final score?
solution: Anu, Cyrus and Ehsan all have 23 ⇒ 3.
fast: Use totals: Anu 38 − 9 − 6, Cyrus 38 − 9 − 6, Ehsan 36 − 8 − 5.
trap: Using averages of all five scores instead of trimmed sums.
note: Rule-based scoring: apply the rule exactly as stated.

text: Suppose J3's scores are disregarded completely and each final score is computed from the remaining four judges by dropping one highest and one lowest and adding the other two. Who would then have the highest final score?
options: Anu
Dia
Ehsan
Bala
solution: Highest: Bala (17).
fast: Recompute the middle two of four for each finalist.
hint: J3 gave Bala the lowest score (5).
trap: Keeping Dia as the winner without recomputing.
note: Changing the panel can reverse rankings — recompute, don't adjust.

text: Which judge gave the highest total score across all five finalists?
options: J1
J4
J3
J2
solution: Judge totals: J1 38, J2 38, J3 38, J4 39, J5 38 ⇒ J4.
fast: Column sums.
trap: Picking J5 because of the single 10.
note: Column totals reveal judge leniency.

text: If only Bala's score from J3 could be changed (from 5 to some other whole number from 1 to 10), what is the minimum value it must be changed to so that Bala has the highest final score outright?
solution: Bala needs a trimmed sum above Dia's 25.
Minimum = 9.
fast: Raising a low score only helps once it enters the middle three.
trap: Answering 8 (that only ties with Dia).
note: Outright winner means strictly greater.

text: In which year was the profit margin the highest?
fast: Compare profit/revenue; 40/160 = 1/4 beats 45/200 = 0.225.
trap: Choosing 2024 (highest absolute profit).
note: Absolute vs relative: read what the question measures.

text: In which year did revenue grow the fastest (in percentage terms) over the previous year?
hint: Divide the change by the previous year's value.
trap: Choosing 2024 for the largest absolute jump (+50).
note: Low base years inflate percentage growth.

text: What was the company's total profit (in ₹ crore) over the six years?
fast: Total revenue 870 − total expenses 715 = 155.
trap: Arithmetic slips; cross-check with total revenue − total expenses.
note: Σ(R − E) = ΣR − ΣE.

text: In how many of the years 2020–2024 did expenses grow at a higher percentage rate than revenue (compared with the previous year)?
solution: 2020: revenue −16.7%, expenses −5% ⇒ expenses 'grew' faster (a smaller fall) ✓.
Answer: 2.
fast: A smaller fall counts as higher growth (−5% > −16.7%).
trap: Ignoring 2020 because both figures fell.
note: Signed comparisons: −5% is greater than −16.7%.

text: Suppose that in 2025 revenue increases by the same absolute amount as it did in 2024, while expenses remain at the 2024 level. What will the 2025 profit be (in ₹ crore)?
solution: 2024 revenue increase = 200 − 150 = 50 ⇒ 2025 revenue = 250.
Expenses = 155 ⇒ profit = 95.
fast: Absolute increase, not percentage.
trap: Using 33.3% growth (revenue 266.7).
note: 'Same amount' = absolute; 'same rate' = percentage.

text: For how many channels did the spending in rupees stay exactly the same from 2023 to 2024?
solution: 2023 (₹ lakh): TV 12, Digital 14, Print 6, Radio 4, Events 4.
2024: TV 12, Digital 22, Print 5, Radio 4, Events 7.
Unchanged: TV and Radio ⇒ 2.
fast: Convert percentages to rupees before comparing.
hint: Shares fell for TV and Radio, but the budget grew.
trap: Comparing percentages directly (none unchanged).
note: Pie charts with different totals: compare amounts, not shares.

text: By what percentage did spending on Digital increase from 2023 to 2024?
solution: 14 → 22 lakh ⇒ increase 8/14 = 57.1%.
trap: Using share change 35 → 44 (25.7%).
note: Share growth ≠ amount growth when totals differ.

text: Which channel had the largest percentage increase in spending (in rupees)?
options: TV
Digital
Events
Print
solution: TV 0%, Digital +57.1%, Print −16.7%, Radio 0%, Events 4 → 7 = +75% ⇒ Events.
fast: Small bases grow fastest: 4 → 7.
trap: Picking Digital for the biggest absolute rise.
note: Percentage leaders often have small bases.

text: What percentage of the combined two-year budget was spent on Print and Radio together?
solution: Print + Radio = (6 + 4) + (5 + 4) = 19 lakh out of 90 lakh = 21.1%.
fast: Sum amounts over both years, then divide by 90.
trap: Averaging the two years' shares (21.5%).
note: Averages of percentages need weights.

text: In 2025 the total budget is 20% higher than in 2024 and TV spending in rupees is the same as in 2024. What is TV's share (in %) of the 2025 budget?
fast: Share = constant amount ÷ new total.
trap: Keeping the share at 24%.
note: Constant amount + growing total ⇒ falling share.

text: How many women work in the firm?
solution: Department sizes: Sales 240, Tech 320, Ops 160, HR 80.
fast: Build a small table: size × women %.
trap: Averaging the four percentages (42.5% ⇒ 340).
note: Weighted, not simple, averages for combined groups.

text: Which department has the largest number of women?
options: Sales
Ops
Tech
HR
solution: Women: Sales 60, Tech 112, Ops 80, HR 48 ⇒ Tech.
fast: Headcount, not percentage.
trap: Choosing HR (highest percentage).
note: Rate leaders are not always count leaders.

text: What percentage of the employees in Sales and Tech combined are men?
trap: Averaging 75% and 65% (70%).
note: Combined % = combined count ÷ combined base.

text: If 40 new women join Sales and nobody leaves, what percentage of Sales will be women?
fast: Both numerator and denominator rise by 40.
trap: Using 100/240 = 41.7% (forgetting the base grows).
note: Additions change the base.

text: How many men must leave Tech (with no one joining) so that women make up exactly 40% of Tech?
solution: Women in Tech = 112 (unchanged). For 40%, Tech size = 112/0.4 = 280.
Men must fall from 208 to 168 ⇒ 40 leave.
fast: Fix the unchanged group and solve for the new total.
trap: Computing 5% of 320 (16), treating a percentage-point change as proportional.
note: Hold the constant group fixed; rescale the total.

text: What was Bharat's share of the profit (in ₹ lakh)?
solution: Capital-months: Aditi 6 × 12 = 72; Bharat 8 × 6 + 6 × 6 = 84; Chetna 9 × 8 = 72.
Distributable profit = 20 − 1 = 19 ⇒ Bharat = 7.
fast: Divide capital-months by 12 to get 6 : 7 : 6.
hint: Chetna's money was in for only 8 months.
trap: Using 12 months for Chetna or ignoring Bharat's withdrawal.
note: Partnership: profit ∝ capital × time; pay fixed amounts first.

text: What is the ratio of Aditi's total earnings from the business to Chetna's?
solution: Aditi = 1 (fixed) + 6 = 7; Chetna = 6 ⇒ 7 : 6.
fast: Add the fixed payment only to Aditi.
hint: Include the working partner's fixed payment.
trap: Answering 1 : 1 by using only the capital-month shares.
note: Total earnings = fixed payment + share.

text: If Bharat had not withdrawn any money, what would Chetna's share of the profit have been?
options: ₹5.4 lakh
₹6 lakh
₹6.3 lakh
₹5.7 lakh
solution: Chetna = 19 × 3/10 = ₹5.7 lakh.
fast: Recompute only Bharat's capital-months.
trap: Keeping the denominator 19 from the original ratio.
note: Any change to one partner changes everyone's fraction.

text: With the same investments and the same ₹1 lakh fixed payment, what is the minimum annual profit (in ₹ lakh) for which Chetna's share would be at least ₹9 lakh?
solution: Chetna gets 6/19 of (P − 1).
fast: Chetna's fraction of the distributable profit is 6/19.
trap: Forgetting to add back the fixed payment (28.5).
note: Reverse questions: solve for the total, then add fixed parts.

text: What percentage of the total profit of ₹20 lakh went to Bharat?
fast: Share ÷ total profit.
hint: Use the ₹20 lakh total, not ₹19 lakh.
trap: Dividing by 19 (36.8%).
note: Read the base of the percentage carefully.

text: How many students take all three electives?
solution: Students taking at least one = 200 − 60 = 140.
140 = 75 + 63 + 55 − 23 − 18 − 20 + (all three) = 132 + (all three) ⇒ all three = 8.
fast: Inclusion–exclusion solved for the triple overlap.
hint: Find the number taking at least one elective first.
trap: Forgetting to subtract the 60 who take none.
note: |A∪B∪C| = ΣA − Σ(pairs) + (all three).

text: How many students take exactly one elective?
solution: Pair-only regions: F&M 15, M&O 10, F&O 12.
Exactly one = 95.
fast: Exactly one = at-least-one − exactly-two − all-three = 140 − 37 − 8.
hint: Subtract the triple overlap from each pair count first.
trap: Using the pair totals (which include the triple) directly.
note: Fill Venn regions from the centre outward.

text: How many students take exactly two electives?
fast: Σ pairs − 3 × (all three).
hint: Remove the all-three students from each pair.
trap: Subtracting the triple only once (53).
note: Exactly two = Σ|pairs| − 3|all three|.

text: How many students take Finance but not Operations?
solution: Finance − (Finance ∩ Operations) = 75 − 20 = 55.
trap: Subtracting only the F&O-only region (12) ⇒ 63.
note: A but not B = |A| − |A∩B|.

text: If 10 students who take only Marketing also add Operations, how many students will take at least two electives?
solution: Currently exactly two = 37, all three = 8 ⇒ 45.
The 10 move from 'only Marketing' to 'Marketing & Operations' ⇒ 55.
fast: They each move from 1 elective to 2.
trap: Adding them to the all-three region.
note: Transfers change two regions: one loses, one gains.

text: What is the minimum possible number of respondents who use all three apps?
solution: Let x₁, x₂, x₃ = numbers using exactly 1, 2, 3 apps. x₁ + x₂ + x₃ = 100 and x₁ + 2x₂ + 3x₃ = 225.
Subtracting: x₂ + 2x₃ = 125. Also x₁ = x₃ − 25 ≥ 0 ⇒ x₃ ≥ 25.
Achievable with x₁ = 0, x₂ = 75, x₃ = 25.
fast: Minimum triple = Σ − 2N = 225 − 200 = 25.
trap: Answering 0 or using Σ − N = 125.
note: Exactly-k equations: Σx_k = N, Σk·x_k = Σ|sets|.

text: What is the maximum possible number of respondents who use all three apps?
solution: From x₂ + 2x₃ = 125, x₂ ≥ 0 ⇒ x₃ ≤ 62 (x₂ must be odd when x₃ = 62: x₂ = 1).
Check feasibility: x₃ = 62, one person uses exactly two apps (e.g. Alpha & Beta), x₁ = 37: Alpha-only 17, Beta-only 12, Gamma-only 8 ✓.
Maximum = 62.
fast: x₃ ≤ ⌊125/2⌋ and ≤ the smallest set (70); the first binds.
trap: Answering 70 (the smallest set), which breaks the total of 100.
note: Max of the triple is limited by both the smallest set and the counting equation.

text: What is the maximum possible number of respondents who use exactly one app?
solution: x₁ = x₃ − 25, so x₁ is largest when x₃ is largest (62) ⇒ x₁ = 37.
fast: Express x₁ in terms of x₃.
trap: Trying to set x₃ = 0 to free up people (infeasible: x₁ would be −25).
note: In these systems, one variable often controls all the others.

text: If exactly 30 respondents use all three apps, how many use exactly two?
fast: Plug into x₂ + 2x₃ = 125.
trap: Using 100 − 30 = 70 (ignores exactly-one users).
note: Derived equations turn 'if' questions into one-line answers.

text: If no respondent uses exactly one app, how many use exactly two apps?
fast: x₁ = 0 fixes x₃ = 25.
trap: Answering 25 (that is the all-three count).
note: Chain the two derived relations.

text: Who is posted in Delhi?
options: Uma
Sunil
Ravi
Tara
solution: Uma sold 40 and is not in Delhi; Ravi is in Chennai. If Uma were in Kolkata she would have sold 10 ✗. So Uma is in Mumbai, and Tara sold 40 − 10 = 30 (clue 1).
Ravi and Sunil share 10 and 20 with Sunil < Ravi ⇒ Ravi 20, Sunil 10.
The Kolkata seller sold 10 ⇒ Sunil is in Kolkata, leaving Tara in Delhi.
fast: Uma's city is forced first; everything cascades from clue 1.
trap: Putting Uma in Kolkata without checking clue 4.
note: Hybrid sets: finish the logic grid before touching the numbers.

text: What was the total revenue (in ₹) from all four salespeople?
fast: Units × city price, then add.
trap: Using the wrong city price for a person.
note: Revenue = units × price of that person's city.

text: What were Tara's total earnings (commission plus bonus) in ₹?
solution: Tara's revenue = 15,000 ⇒ commission 750. She sold 30 units ⇒ bonus 1,000.
Total = 1,750.
trap: Leaving out the bonus because Tara did not sell the most.
note: Read inclusive thresholds (≥) carefully.

text: If Ravi and Sunil swapped cities but sold the same numbers of units, how would the total revenue change?
options: Decrease of ₹500
Decrease of ₹1000
Increase of ₹500
No change
solution: Ravi in Kolkata: 20 × 400 = 8,000; Sunil in Chennai: 10 × 450 = 4,500.
fast: Only two terms change: (450 − 400) × (10 − 20) = −500.
trap: Assuming no change because the cities are only exchanged.
note: Swaps change totals when both quantities and prices differ.

text: How many salespeople earned more than ₹500 in total (commission plus bonus)?
solution: Earnings: Ravi 450, Sunil 200, Tara 1,750, Uma 1,200 + 1,000 = 2,200 ⇒ 2.
fast: Only the bonus winners exceed 500 here.
trap: Counting Ravi (₹450 is not more than ₹500).
note: Strict vs non-strict comparisons matter.

text: Which family lives on floor 4?
options: Nair
Mehta
Oberoi
Pillai
solution: Clue 1 and 5: Nair on 2 or 3 with Oberoi on 4 or 5.
If Nair = 3, Oberoi = 5 and Qureshi = 1; the floor-3 family (Nair) has 5 members, so Oberoi would need 7 ✗.
So Nair = 2, Oberoi = 4, and Mehta/Pillai/Qureshi take floors 1, 3, 5.
Floor 3 has 5 members; it can't be Qureshi (1 member) or Pillai (fewer than Mehta) ⇒ Mehta on 3, so Pillai on 1 and Qureshi on 5.
Members: Qureshi 1, Mehta 5; Nair and Oberoi differ by 2 from {2, 3, 4} ⇒ Nair 2, Oberoi 4; Pillai 3.
Floor 4: Oberoi.
fast: Case on Nair's floor; the member clue kills one case immediately.
hint: Nair can only be on floor 2 or 3.
trap: Ignoring the member-count half of clue 1.
note: Two-attribute clues give double leverage — use both halves.

text: How many members does the Pillai family have?
solution: Pillai = 3 (the remaining number after Qureshi 1, Nair 2, Oberoi 4, Mehta 5).
fast: Last remaining value.
trap: Mixing floor numbers with member counts (answering 1).
note: Keep separate rows for each attribute.

text: Which family pays the highest monthly maintenance charge?
options: Mehta
Qureshi
Nair
Oberoi
solution: Highest: Mehta.
fast: Compare 200 × floor + 300 × members only.
hint: Members are weighted more than floors.
trap: Choosing Qureshi for being on the top floor.
note: Drop common constants when comparing.

text: What is the total monthly maintenance collected from all five families (in ₹)?
fast: Floors and members each sum to 15.
hint: Use the sums of floors and members.
trap: Arithmetic slips; the shortcut avoids them.
note: Totals of linear rules can use aggregate sums.

text: If the per-floor rate were ₹300 instead of ₹200 (all else unchanged), how many families would pay more than ₹2,500 a month?
solution: New charges: Pillai 2,200; Nair 2,200; Mehta 3,400; Oberoi 3,400; Qureshi 2,800.
More than 2,500: Mehta, Oberoi, Qureshi ⇒ 3.
fast: Each charge rises by 100 × floor.
hint: Add 100 × floor number to each old charge.
trap: Adding a flat ₹100 to every family.
note: Rate changes scale with the variable they multiply.

text: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?
options: Attention platforms steal time that users would otherwise spend productively.
Users of free platforms are helpless before the advertisers who fund them.
The deeper harm of attention-driven platforms lies in how they shape behaviour, so remedies must change what these systems are rewarded for.
Time limits and timers are the most practical remedy for excessive screen use.
solution: The author rejects 'theft' as the key problem and says 'The stronger objection is not that attention is taken but that it is shaped.'
The remedy follows: 'A more durable remedy would change what the system is rewarded for'.
A is the view the author calls an imperfect metaphor. D is dismissed as treating 'the symptom'. B contradicts 'None of this requires treating users as helpless.'
fast: Main-idea answers must cover both the diagnosis (shaping) and the prescription (change the reward).
hint: Look for the sentence where the author says which objection is 'stronger'.
trap: Option A borrows the critics' word 'theft', which the author explicitly qualifies.
note: In CAT, the author's position often appears right after 'but' or 'the stronger objection'.
evidence: The stronger objection is not that attention is taken but that it is shaped.
A more durable remedy would change what the system is rewarded for

text: The author mentions television primarily in order to:
options: describe how advertisers refined their tools over the decades.
question the assumption that the time now spent on platforms would otherwise have been used better.
show that television was more harmful than today's platforms.
argue that platforms add no new risks beyond those television posed.
solution: The mention appears inside the argument against the theft metaphor: 'It is not obvious that the hours now spent scrolling would otherwise have gone to reading philosophy or tending gardens; some would have gone to television'.
D overreaches: the author says television used 'far cruder tools', implying today's systems are more powerful. C and A are not claimed.
fast: Ask what claim the example is attached to — here, the claim that 'theft' is imperfect.
hint: Read the sentence before the television reference.
trap: Option D sounds balanced but ignores 'far cruder tools'.
note: Purpose-of-example questions: the example serves the sentence around it.
