evidence: It is not obvious that the hours now spent scrolling would otherwise have gone to reading philosophy or tending gardens; some would have gone to television, which made similar bargains with far cruder tools.

text: Which of the following measures would the author most likely regard as a durable remedy?
options: Paying users a small amount for every hour they spend on a platform.
Judging a recommendation system by how many users later say their session was worthwhile.
Requiring platforms to display a running timer on every screen.
A two-hour daily cap on app usage enforced by the phone's operating system.
solution: The author's durable remedy is to change the reward: 'measuring, say, whether users report that their time was well spent, rather than how much of it was spent.' Option B is exactly this.
D and C are 'limits and timers', which 'treat the symptom'. A still rewards time spent.
fast: Match the option to the author's own example of a durable remedy.
hint: Which option changes what the system is rewarded for?
trap: Choosing D or C because they sound protective; the author calls them symptomatic.
note: Application questions: map each option onto the author's explicit criteria.
evidence: measuring, say, whether users report that their time was well spent, rather than how much of it was spent
time limits treat the symptom while leaving the trainer at work

text: The author's attitude towards people who choose an evening of light entertainment is best described as:
options: contemptuous
respectful of their autonomy
anxious about their well-being
indifferent
solution: The author says such a person 'is exercising, not surrendering, autonomy'. That is respect, not contempt or anxiety.
fast: Find the one sentence about these people and read its verb.
trap: Picking 'anxious' because the passage overall is critical of platforms.
note: Tone questions are about a specific target; don't transfer the passage's general mood.
evidence: a person who chooses an evening of light entertainment is exercising, not surrendering, autonomy

text: The passage is primarily concerned with arguing that:
options: street trees are a public-health asset whose value depends on sustained canopy rather than planting counts.
cities should stop planting new trees and focus only on existing ones.
poorer neighbourhoods suffer more from heat because of bad planning decisions made recently.
air conditioning is a better solution to urban heat than trees.
solution: The passage reframes trees as 'a public health service' and concludes they 'should be judged by the canopy it sustains over time rather than by the numbers it announces'.
B contradicts 'None of this means that new planting is futile.' C distorts 'planned generously decades ago' (older, not recent). D is never argued.
fast: The last paragraph usually restates the thesis in balanced form.
trap: Option B takes the maintenance argument to an extreme the author rejects.
note: Watch for extreme options ('only', 'stop') in main-idea questions.
evidence: it is a public health service
urban forestry should be judged by the canopy it sustains over time rather than by the numbers it announces at a ceremony

text: Which of the following can be inferred about a city that fells mature trees to widen a road and plants five saplings for each tree removed?
options: The city will have more shade within a few years.
The city has violated its planting targets.
The street is likely to be hotter for many years despite the higher tree count.
The saplings will certainly die within a few years.
solution: The author says such a swap 'may look like a net gain on paper while leaving the street measurably hotter for a generation.'
A contradicts the decade-long delay. B is irrelevant. D overstates: 'a large share' die, not all.
fast: The passage states this almost directly.
trap: Option D turns 'a large share' into 'certainly'.
note: Inference answers stay within what the text supports; beware absolute words.
evidence: Felling a mature tree to widen a road and replacing it with five saplings may look like a net gain on paper while leaving the street measurably hotter for a generation.

text: According to the passage, why is the heat stored by asphalt particularly harmful?
options: It is released at night, when the body most needs to cool down.
It evaporates water from leaves.
It damages the roots of nearby trees.
It raises the cost of air conditioning in wealthy areas.
solution: 'the heat it stores is released well into the night, when the human body most needs to cool down.'
fast: Detail question: locate and match.
trap: Option B confuses the cooling mechanism of trees with the heating of asphalt.
note: For detail questions, paraphrase the exact line.
evidence: the heat it stores is released well into the night, when the human body most needs to cool down

text: The author's comment that a city may 'spend heavily to create a statistic' suggests that the author regards large planting targets as:
options: irrelevant to the problem of urban heat.
a sensible first step that guarantees future shade.
fraudulent attempts to mislead citizens.
potentially more useful for publicity than for actual cooling.
solution: The author contrasts announced numbers with real canopy: planting targets can yield a statistic without shade, and maintenance is 'a far less photogenic activity'.
C ('fraudulent') is too strong; A contradicts 'None of this means that new planting is futile.'
fast: Pick the moderate reading of the author's irony.
hint: Note the contrast with 'less photogenic' maintenance.
trap: Choosing 'fraudulent' — the author is sceptical, not accusatory.
note: CAT tone answers are usually moderate: sceptical > hostile.
evidence: A city that plants a million trees and loses half of them has spent heavily to create a statistic.
a far less photogenic activity

text: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?
options: Translation mainly loses the economy, rhythm and texture of the original, not its meaning, so translators must recreate those qualities.
Some words in every language are genuinely impossible to translate.
Critics of translated novels are usually mistaken when they say something is missing.
Translators should aim to produce exact replicas of the original text.
solution: 'What cannot be carried over intact is not meaning but economy', and the loss 'is rhythmic and textural rather than conceptual'. Translators must 'reinvent rather than transfer' such features.
B is the view the author debunks. C distorts: critics are 'often right, but usually wrong about what'. D contradicts the musician analogy.
fast: The thesis is the reversal of the popular view in paragraph 1.
hint: Find what, according to the author, is actually lost.
trap: Option C misreads 'often right, but usually wrong about what'.
note: Contrarian passages: the main idea is the author's correction, not the view being corrected.
evidence: What cannot be carried over intact is not meaning but economy.
The loss, in other words, is rhythmic and textural rather than conceptual.

text: The author would most likely agree that a critic who says a translated novel 'misses something':
options: is always wrong, because meaning can always be carried over.
is usually correct that the translator misunderstood key ideas.
is usually correct that something is lost, though mistaken about what it is.
should read the novel only in the original language.
solution: 'A critic who complains that a translated novel "misses something" is often right, but usually wrong about what.' The missing element is 'the pace at which ideas were delivered', not an idea.
fast: Near-quotation from paragraph 3.
hint: Read the sentence about the critic closely.
trap: Option B is exactly what the author says the critic gets wrong.
note: Two-part claims ('right, but wrong about what') are favourite CAT traps.
evidence: is often right, but usually wrong about what
The missing element is rarely an idea the translator failed to grasp

text: The comparison of translators to musicians transposing a piece into a different key is used to suggest that:
options: translation requires technical skill similar to engineering.
music is easier to translate than literature.
translated texts should be read aloud to be appreciated.
a good translation may alter individual elements so that the whole produces an equivalent effect.
solution: 'Some notes must move... The test of success is not whether every element survives but whether the whole still moves the listener as the original did.'
A inverts the contrast: translators are 'less like engineers'.
fast: The analogy's point is stated in the next sentence.
hint: Look at 'The test of success is...'.
trap: Option A picks the rejected half of the comparison.
note: When an analogy has two halves (engineer vs musician), note which one the author endorses.
evidence: The test of success is not whether every element survives but whether the whole still moves the listener as the original did.
less like engineers building an exact replica

text: The author's attitude towards lists of 'untranslatable' words is best described as:
options: neutral and uncommitted
enthusiastic endorsement
openly hostile
gently sceptical
solution: The author calls the lists 'charming' but says they 'get the matter backwards' — sceptical without hostility.
fast: 'Charming' + 'gets the matter backwards' = mild scepticism.
hint: Note both the compliment and the criticism.
trap: 'Openly hostile' ignores 'charming'.
note: Mixed signals usually point to a moderate tone.
evidence: Such lists are charming
the romance of the untranslatable word gets the matter backwards

text: Which of the following best summarises the passage?
options: Comparative viewing of art from many civilisations is the main public benefit of large museums.
Loans of disputed objects are a disguised way for museums to keep ownership.
Museums in former imperial capitals acquired their collections illegally and must return them.
The universal-museum defence is being challenged by a focus on present justice, producing a range of arrangements beyond simple keeping or returning.
solution: The passage moves from the universality defence, to its 'peculiar structure', to the shift towards 'whether continued possession is just now', and to experiments showing 'the old binary... no longer describes' the options.
C contradicts the point that acquisitions were often legal at the time. A and B are single details.
fast: A summary must span the defence, the critique and the new range of responses.
hint: Track the passage's movement paragraph by paragraph.
trap: Option C — the passage explicitly separates legality then from justice now.
note: Summary answers cover the arc of the passage, not one paragraph.
evidence: whether continued possession is just now
the old binary—keep everything or give everything back—no longer describes the actual field of possibilities

text: Why, according to the passage, has the debate shifted from legality at the time of acquisition to justice in the present?
options: Because museums have admitted that all their acquisitions were illegal.
Because historical records of acquisitions have been lost.
Because the legality question often favours museums, while present justice cannot be settled by old documents and requires a current judgement.
Because international law now forbids museums from holding foreign objects.
solution: 'the first question can often be answered in the museum's favour... while the second cannot be settled by consulting old documents. It requires a judgement about relationships in the present.'
fast: Paraphrase paragraph 3.
trap: Option D invents a legal change never mentioned.
note: Causal questions: find 'because/therefore/the shift matters because'.
evidence: the first question can often be answered in the museum's favour
the second cannot be settled by consulting old documents

text: The author's treatment of the 'universality' argument can best be described as:
options: neutral, since the author does not evaluate it.
dismissive, since the argument has no merit.
acknowledging its partial validity while exposing an imbalance in how it works in practice.
fully supportive, since comparison is a public good.
solution: 'The argument is not empty' (partial validity) but it 'has a peculiar structure' in which one set of cities 'hosts the world while the rest of the world must travel'.
fast: 'Not empty… But…' signals a concession followed by a critique.
trap: Choosing 'dismissive' by ignoring the concession.
note: Concession + critique = balanced but critical.
evidence: The argument is not empty.
one set of cities hosts the world while the rest of the world must travel

text: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the universal museum's defence as presented in the passage?
options: Visitors to large museums report that side-by-side displays deepened their understanding.
Some returned objects have been displayed in newly built local museums.
Digital high-resolution displays let viewers anywhere compare objects from many civilisations as effectively as seeing them together in one building.
Many objects in large museums were acquired legally under the laws of the time.
solution: The defence rests on the comparative encounter being 'a public good that would be lost if collections were dispersed'. If comparison no longer requires physical co-location, dispersal would not lose that good.
A strengthens the defence. D concerns legality, not universality. B is about returns, not the defence's premise.
fast: Attack the premise: 'would be lost if collections were dispersed'.
hint: What does the defence assume must stay together?
trap: Option D is true per the passage but does not bear on universality.
note: Weaken = break the link between premise and conclusion.
evidence: this comparative encounter is itself a public good that would be lost if collections were dispersed

text: The passage is best described as:
options: a demonstration that placebo effects are entirely statistical illusions.
an argument that placebos can cure serious diseases through the power of the mind.
a balanced account that separates statistical artefacts from genuine expectation effects and draws a lesson about how care is delivered.
a criticism of clinical trials for using placebo groups.
solution: The author subtracts regression ('Part of this improvement is statistical'), affirms a residue ('What remains, however, is not nothing'), warns against 'two opposite errors', and concludes that 'The manner in which care is delivered is itself part of the treatment'.
B and A are the two errors. D is not argued.
fast: The 'two opposite errors' paragraph tells you the author sits in the middle.
hint: Which options match the two errors the author rejects?
trap: Picking A after reading only paragraph 2.
note: Balanced passages: eliminate both extremes.
evidence: Part of this improvement is statistical rather than psychological.
What remains, however, is not nothing.
The manner in which care is delivered is itself part of the treatment

text: According to the passage, why might a group of trial patients appear to improve even if they receive no treatment at all?
options: Because placebos contain small amounts of active ingredients.
Because patients are told that their pills are inert.
Because doctors pay more attention to patients in trials.
Because patients often enrol when symptoms are at their worst, and extreme symptoms tend on average to become less severe on their own.
solution: Paragraph 2: 'Patients tend to enrol in trials when their symptoms are at their worst, and symptoms that are unusually severe tend, on average, to become less severe on their own.'
fast: This is regression to the mean.
trap: Option C is a real factor but the question says 'no treatment at all'.
note: Know regression to the mean: extreme first measurements drift back toward average.
evidence: Patients tend to enrol in trials when their symptoms are at their worst

text: Which of the following statements would the author most likely reject?
options: Evidence that placebos change objective measures of disease is thin.
Because placebo relief comes from expectation, it should not count as genuine improvement.
Shorter consultations may remove part of what makes treatment work.
Relief from pain caused by expectation is still real relief.
solution: The author calls dismissing placebo relief 'as mere illusion' an error: relief a patient 'genuinely feels' is not 'less real because its cause was an expectation'. D, A, C are all endorsed.
fast: 'Reject' questions: find the option matching an error the author names.
trap: Rushing and picking A, which the author actually asserts.
note: EXCEPT/reject questions: verify each option against the text.
evidence: The other is to dismiss it as mere illusion
the evidence for effects on objective measures of disease is thin

text: In the passage, the phrase 'an ingredient it never learned to measure' refers to:
options: the contribution that the manner of care makes to treatment outcomes.
the costs of running clinical trials.
an undisclosed chemical in placebo pills.
the natural fluctuation of symptoms over time.
solution: It follows 'The manner in which care is delivered is itself part of the treatment'; shortening consultations discards that ingredient.
fast: Read the sentence the phrase completes.
trap: Taking 'ingredient' literally (option A).
note: Metaphors in the last line usually point back to the passage's thesis.
evidence: The manner in which care is delivered is itself part of the treatment

text: Which of the following best states the author's explanation for the decline of repair?
options: Repair technicians have lost their skills because of automation.
Consumers no longer value durability.
A combination of cheap manufacturing, costly local labour and individually reasonable design choices has made repair uneconomic or impossible.
Manufacturers deliberately design most products to fail early.
solution: The author calls planned obsolescence only part of the story and offers a 'fuller explanation' involving 'decisions that are individually reasonable': cheap manufacturing vs costly labour (paragraph 2) and design choices that 'Together... produce a world in which repair is gradually designed out'.
D is the partial explanation the author goes beyond. A reverses cause and effect.
fast: The 'fuller explanation' has two parts: arithmetic + design.
hint: What does the author contrast with planned obsolescence?
trap: Option D — documented cases exist, but the author calls it the less complete account.
note: When a passage says 'the fuller explanation', the answer is that fuller account.
evidence: the fuller explanation is less conspiratorial and in some ways more troubling, because it involves decisions that are individually reasonable
Together they produce a world in which repair is gradually designed out.

text: Why does the author describe the fuller explanation as 'more troubling' than planned obsolescence?
options: Because it shows that repair was never economical.
Because it proves that manufacturers lie about safety.
Because it implies that consumers are to blame.
Because no single bad actor is responsible, so the problem cannot be fixed simply by punishing deceptive firms.
solution: The fuller explanation 'involves decisions that are individually reasonable' and costs that 'fall on no single buyer or seller'. With no villain, there is no simple target.
fast: 'Individually reasonable' is the key phrase.
hint: Why is a problem with no villain harder?
trap: Option C — the passage does not blame consumers.
note: Inference questions often hinge on a single qualifying phrase.
evidence: decisions that are individually reasonable
Because these costs fall on no single buyer or seller

text: According to the passage, the most effective right-to-repair proposals aim to:
options: ban glued components.
require consumers to repair products before replacing them.
require access to manuals, spare parts and diagnostic tools so that repair remains possible.
make repair cheaper than replacement by law.
solution: 'They aim instead at the design and information choices—requiring access to manuals, spare parts and diagnostic tools'. D and B are what they do not do ('not... by decree', 'not to mandate a behaviour').
fast: Locate the last paragraph.
hint: What do they 'not try' to do?
trap: Option D is explicitly rejected.
note: Detail questions often include the explicitly denied option as a trap.
evidence: requiring access to manuals, spare parts and diagnostic tools
The aim is to restore an option, not to mandate a behaviour.

text: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that repair economics are driven largely by the gap between manufacturing and labour costs?
options: Many consumers say they prefer new products to repaired ones.
Electronic waste has grown rapidly in recent decades.
Some manufacturers have been fined for deliberately shortening product life.
In countries where technicians' wages are low relative to product prices, small appliances are repaired far more often.
solution: If repair rates rise where labour is cheap relative to products, that directly supports the cost-gap explanation.
A is about preference. C supports planned obsolescence, the rival explanation. B is a consequence, not a cause.
fast: A strengthener shows the proposed cause varying with the effect.
hint: Look for an option that varies labour cost and observes repair.
trap: Option C supports the rival explanation.
note: Natural experiments (cause varies → effect varies) are the strongest strengtheners.
evidence: Labour in the places where products are used has not become cheap in the same way.
For many goods the arithmetic simply favours replacement

text: The passage is primarily concerned with:
options: explaining the problem of moral luck and outlining different responses to it, along with a practical implication.
proving that outcomes should never affect moral judgement.
arguing that drunk driving should be punished more severely.
criticising philosophers for ignoring legal practice.
solution: The passage defines moral luck, sets out three responses, and ends with 'the problem has a practical edge' for legal systems.
B is only one of the responses, which the author does not endorse. C and D are not the passage's concern.
fast: Descriptive/survey passages: the answer names the problem and the range of responses.
hint: Count how many positions the passage presents.
trap: Picking B, which is one position, not the author's thesis.
note: Survey passages rarely endorse one extreme view.
evidence: Philosophers call this the problem of moral luck.
Whatever position one takes, the problem has a practical edge.

text: According to the third position described in the passage, how do the two drivers differ?
options: Neither driver is blameworthy, because outcomes are outside their control.
They are equally blameworthy, but only the second bears responsibility for a death, with obligations that follow from it.
The first driver is more blameworthy because he escaped consequences.
The second driver is more blameworthy because his act caused harm.
solution: 'Both drivers, it holds, are equally blameworthy for the reckless choice. But only the second is responsible for a death, and responsibility brings obligations'.
fast: Blame (same) vs responsibility (different).
trap: Option D describes ordinary feeling, not the third position.
note: Distinctions (blame vs responsibility) are prime CAT targets.
evidence: Both drivers, it holds, are equally blameworthy for the reckless choice.
But only the second is responsible for a death

text: According to the passage, the contradiction at the heart of moral luck arises because:
options: careless acts are always punished by chance.
the law and ordinary feeling disagree about careless drivers.
people should be judged only for what they control, yet outcomes—which are rarely fully controlled—seem to matter to judgement.
philosophers cannot agree on the definition of blame.
solution: The two beliefs: judge only what is controlled; outcomes matter. 'together they generate a contradiction, because outcomes are almost never entirely within anyone's control.'
B is false — 'the law usually agrees' with ordinary feeling.
fast: Name the two beliefs, then the reason they clash.
trap: Option B — the passage says the law usually agrees with people's harsher judgement.
note: State the contradiction in your own words before looking at options.
evidence: The first is that people should be judged only for what is within their control.
because outcomes are almost never entirely within anyone's control

text: The author's view of legal systems that punish outcomes rather than choices is that such systems:
options: are indefensible and should be abolished.
should ignore harms and focus only on intentions.
measure guilt precisely.
may be defensible but should openly acknowledge that they distribute penalties partly by chance.
solution: 'That may be defensible—the law must respond to harms, not only intentions—but it should be acknowledged rather than disguised as a precise measure of guilt.'
fast: Qualified approval + a demand for honesty.
trap: Option B contradicts 'the law must respond to harms, not only intentions'.
note: Look for 'may be… but…' constructions to identify qualified views.
evidence: That may be defensible
it should be acknowledged rather than disguised as a precise measure of guilt

text: Which of the following best describes the structure of the passage?
options: It argues that land-based mining is more harmful than any alternative.
It describes how nodules form and why they contain metals.
It argues forcefully in favour of deep-sea mining.
It presents the case for and against deep-sea mining, identifies the burden of proof under uncertainty as the core disagreement, and notes the asymmetry between acting and waiting.
solution: Paragraph 2 gives supporters' case, paragraph 3 critics', paragraph 4 says 'The disagreement is less about facts than about who should bear the burden of proof', and paragraph 5 notes a decision to open 'would be difficult to reverse; a decision to wait could be revisited.'
fast: Structure questions: map each paragraph to a function.
trap: Option B describes only paragraph 1.
note: The 'crux' sentence usually anchors the structure answer.
evidence: The disagreement is less about facts than about who should bear the burden of proof when facts are missing.
a decision to wait could be revisited

text: The author's final paragraph most strongly implies that:
options: battery chemistry has already changed enough to end demand for nickel and cobalt.
the irreversibility of opening the deep sea gives some extra weight to waiting when forecasts are uncertain.
demand forecasts for metals are certainly exaggerated.
recycling will make mining unnecessary.
solution: The author contrasts a decision 'difficult to reverse' with one that 'could be revisited', given forecasts that 'may change'. That favours waiting under uncertainty without claiming the forecasts are wrong.
C, D and A overstate 'may change'.
fast: The key word is 'reverse'.
hint: Compare the two decisions in the last sentence.
trap: Overstating 'may change' as 'certainly exaggerated'.
note: Asymmetric reversibility is a classic argument pattern.
evidence: A decision taken now to open the deep sea would be difficult to reverse; a decision to wait could be revisited.

text: The author's attitude towards the supporters' argument is best described as:
options: respectful, treating it as serious though contested
sarcastic
dismissive
wholly persuaded
solution: 'Supporters of deep-sea mining make an argument that deserves to be taken seriously.'
fast: One sentence settles it.
trap: Choosing 'wholly persuaded' — the author gives the critics equal weight.
note: Tone: 'deserves to be taken seriously' = respect, not agreement.
evidence: make an argument that deserves to be taken seriously

text: According to the passage, why would species dependent on nodules not recover on a human timescale?
options: Because the species are undescribed.
Because sediment plumes settle only near the collection site.
Because the nodules took millions of years to form.
Because mining would pollute the surface waters.
solution: 'Because the nodules took millions of years to form, any species dependent on them would not recover on any timescale meaningful to humans.'
B contradicts 'drift far from the collection site'.
fast: Direct 'because' clause.
trap: Option B reverses the sediment point.
note: Detail answers often reuse the passage's 'because' clause.
evidence: Because the nodules took millions of years to form

text: Which of the following best captures the author's use of the history of the index?
options: To caution against drawing simple reassurance from the past while raising the question of whose judgement guides our tools.
To prove that worries about search engines are exaggerated.
To argue that search engines should be replaced by indexes.
To show that the index destroyed deep reading.
solution: The author calls the reassuring inference 'too quick' and concludes the history 'offers neither reassurance nor alarm' but a question: 'whose judgement is it, and can we see it?'
B is the inference rejected. D contradicts 'alongside the old kind'.
fast: The conclusion explicitly says 'neither reassurance nor alarm'.
trap: Option B is the 'too quick' inference.
note: When the author labels an argument 'too quick', it's a trap option.
evidence: That inference is too quick.
offers neither reassurance nor alarm

text: Which of the following differences between an index and a search engine does the author emphasise?
options: An index reflects the visible, finite choices of someone who has read the whole book, whereas a search engine ranks text by criteria users cannot inspect.
Indexes cover more topics than search engines.
Search engines are compiled by experts, indexes by amateurs.
An index is faster to use than a search engine.
solution: 'An index is compiled by a person who has read the whole book... Its selections are visible and finite. A search engine ranks... according to criteria its users cannot inspect.'
fast: Visible & finite vs uninspectable & unlimited.
trap: Option B reverses the scale point.
note: Comparison questions: match both halves.
evidence: Its selections are visible and finite.
according to criteria its users cannot inspect

text: What does the author suggest about the effect of the index on readers?
options: It had no real effect on how people read.
It created a new kind of reader skilled at retrieval, alongside readers who still read whole books.
It made readers more likely to memorise texts.
It eliminated cover-to-cover reading entirely.
solution: 'it produced a new kind of reader, adept at retrieval, alongside the old kind who read from cover to cover.'
fast: 'Alongside' rules out 'eliminated'.
trap: Option A — the author says 'The index did change reading'.
note: Watch for 'alongside' vs 'replaced'.
evidence: it produced a new kind of reader, adept at retrieval, alongside the old kind who read from cover to cover

text: In the passage, the phrase 'The complaint has a familiar ring' suggests that:
options: the complaint was made in a musical form.
the complaint was repeated by the same critics many times.
the complaint was correct.
similar complaints are heard today about newer tools.
solution: The next paragraph draws 'The parallel with contemporary anxieties about search engines'.
fast: The following sentence explains the ring.
hint: What does the next paragraph compare it with?
trap: Option C — familiarity says nothing about correctness.
note: Idioms are clarified by the sentences that follow them.
evidence: The parallel with contemporary anxieties about search engines is instructive

text: The central claim of the passage is that automated screening:
options: can reproduce past biases despite its consistency, and its real advantage—measurable unfairness—is realised only if it is actually audited.
is inherently fairer than human recruitment because it is consistent.
should be banned until sensitive attributes are removed from all data.
is inherently more biased than human recruitment.
solution: 'Consistency, in this setting, is not the same as fairness.' 'The real advantage of automation, then, is not that it is fair by default but that its unfairness can be measured—if anyone is permitted to look.'
D contradicts 'None of this shows that automated screening is worse'. C — removing attributes 'helps less than one might hope'.
fast: The thesis has a conditional: '…if anyone is permitted to look'.
trap: Option B is the promoters' view the author challenges.
note: Keep the author's qualifications in the answer.
evidence: Consistency, in this setting, is not the same as fairness.
The real advantage of automation, then, is not that it is fair by default but that its unfairness can be measured

text: Why does removing sensitive attributes from the data help 'less than one might hope'?
options: Because other features can correlate with the removed attributes and let the system reconstruct them indirectly.
Because the law requires those attributes to be kept.
Because recruiters add the attributes back manually.
Because the system stops working without them.
solution: 'Other features... may correlate with the removed attributes and allow the system to reconstruct them indirectly.'
fast: Proxy variables.
trap: Inventing reasons (law, manual re-entry) not in the passage.
note: Proxy discrimination: blindness ≠ neutrality.
evidence: may correlate with the removed attributes and allow the system to reconstruct them indirectly

text: Which of the following tests best fits the kind of audit the author describes?
options: Removing age and gender from the training data.
Asking recruiters whether they trust the software.
Submitting two applications identical except for the applicant's postal code and checking whether their rankings differ.
Comparing the software's hiring rate with last year's hiring rate.
solution: 'one can submit matched applications that differ in a single feature and observe whether the ranking changes.' Option C does exactly this.
fast: Matched pairs, one difference.
trap: Option A is the attribute-removal fix, not an audit.
note: Controlled comparisons isolate a single variable.
evidence: one can submit matched applications that differ in a single feature and observe whether the ranking changes

text: The tone of the final paragraph is best described as:
options: celebratory
indifferent
cautiously sceptical
despairing
solution: 'The promise of auditable fairness is real, but it is a promise about what could be done, not about what is being done.' — measured scepticism.
fast: 'Real, but…' = cautious.
hint: Note both halves of the last sentence.
trap: 'Despairing' overstates; the promise is called 'real'.
note: Moderate tone words usually win.
evidence: The promise of auditable fairness is real, but it is a promise about what could be done, not about what is being done.

text: Which of the following best states the author's position on mathematical beauty?
options: It matters only to mathematicians who are also interested in art.
It is an affectation borrowed from art criticism.
It is a trained, usually reliable signal of explanatory and fruitful ideas, though fallible and no substitute for checking.
It is an infallible guide to truth.
solution: 'Beauty, on this view, is a kind of compressed judgement about fruitfulness', but 'It would be a mistake... to treat aesthetic judgement as infallible', ending with 'never a substitute for checking'.
B is the outsiders' view rejected in paragraph 1; A contradicts 'too many people who are otherwise indifferent to art'.
fast: The final paragraph states the 'most defensible position'.
trap: Option D ignores paragraph 4.
note: Final 'most defensible position' sentences are usually the thesis.
evidence: Beauty, on this view, is a kind of compressed judgement about fruitfulness.
never a substitute for checking

text: According to the passage, why might a computer-assisted proof that checks thousands of cases be considered unsatisfying?
options: Because it is too short.
Because it verifies the result without revealing why it is true.
Because computers cannot handle geometry.
Because it may contain errors.
solution: 'A proof that checks thousands of cases by computer may be entirely convincing and still be called unsatisfying, because it leaves the reason hidden.'
fast: Explain vs verify.
trap: Option D — the passage says such a proof may be 'entirely convincing'.
note: Contrast pairs (explain/verify) are frequent RC targets.
evidence: because it leaves the reason hidden

text: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as a feature of a beautiful proof?
options: It is short relative to what it establishes.
It connects areas that seemed unrelated.
It uses only methods that are already widely admired.
It explains why a result must be true.
solution: Shortness, connection and explanation are listed. Relying on admired methods is mentioned only as a risk ('Taste can also be conservative').
fast: Tick off the three listed features.
trap: Choosing an option that is listed because it sounds less 'beautiful'.
note: NOT questions: verify each option against the text.
evidence: A beautiful proof is usually short relative to what it establishes.
Taste can also be conservative

text: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the claim that beauty is 'a kind of compressed judgement about fruitfulness'?
options: Most mathematicians enjoy music.
Computer proofs are becoming more common.
Proofs rated as elegant by mathematicians are, on average, cited and extended in later work more often than proofs rated as inelegant.
Some elegant proofs have contained errors.
solution: If elegant proofs are more often extended later, elegance does track fruitfulness. D weakens (fallibility). A and B are irrelevant.
fast: Find evidence that 'elegant' predicts 'fruitful'.
trap: Option D is in the passage but cuts the other way.
note: Strengtheners show the claimed correlation actually holds.
evidence: Proofs that explain tend to generalise

text: The author's main purpose in the passage is to:
options: argue that written archives are useless to historians.
describe the use of rhythm in poetry.
challenge the view of oral traditions as fragile, while showing that both oral and written sources are selective in ways historians must account for.
show that oral traditions preserve all information perfectly.
solution: Paragraph 1 challenges the 'fragile archives' image; paragraph 3 notes selectivity; paragraph 4 says 'written archives are selective too'; the conclusion asks what each source 'was designed to remember'.
D contradicts 'None of this means that oral traditions preserve everything unchanged.'
fast: The answer must include both the challenge and the balancing point.
hint: Read the first and last paragraphs together.
trap: Option D overstates the author's defence.
note: Balanced conclusions usually beat extreme ones.
evidence: The image owes more to the habits of literate cultures than to evidence.
But written archives are selective too.

text: According to the passage, how does an audience help preserve an oral tradition?
options: By inventing new details to keep the story interesting.
By writing the story down after each performance.
By paying the performer to memorise the text.
By correcting errors in real time, acting as a distributed editor.
solution: 'an audience that has heard a story many times acts as a distributed editor, correcting errors in real time.'
fast: Direct match.
trap: Option A is the opposite of preservation.
note: Detail: find the sentence, paraphrase, match.
evidence: acts as a distributed editor, correcting errors in real time

text: Which of the following would the author most likely expect an oral tradition to preserve most accurately?
options: The names of foreign traders who once passed through.
The rights of particular families to use a piece of land.
The weather on the day a village was founded.
The exact sequence of battles fought many centuries ago.
solution: 'Details that serve a community's present needs—claims to land, obligations between families... —are guarded closely', while the tradition may be 'quite unreliable about the order of events centuries ago.'
fast: Present use ⇒ preserved.
hint: What does a community still need?
trap: Option D is precisely what the author says may be unreliable.
note: Selective preservation follows present purpose.
evidence: claims to land, obligations between families
quite unreliable about the order of events centuries ago

text: According to the author, why is the selectivity of written archives 'less visible'?
options: Because historians refuse to study archives.
Because documents carry an air of neutrality that spoken performances do not claim.
Because archives record everything.
Because archives are stored in inaccessible places.
solution: 'documents carry an air of neutrality that a spoken performance does not claim.' C contradicts the whole paragraph.
fast: Direct 'because' clause.
trap: Option C contradicts 'written archives are selective too'.
note: Watch for options that deny the paragraph's premise.
evidence: documents carry an air of neutrality that a spoken performance does not claim

text: Which of the following best summarises the author's position?
options: The four-day week has been proven to work in all industries.
Trial results are encouraging but limited by self-selection and an unclear mechanism, so the real questions concern which kinds of work, over what period and with what wider effects.
Firms should cut meetings rather than working hours.
The four-day week is a failed experiment.
solution: 'The results deserve attention, but they also deserve scrutiny.' The author cites non-random samples and the mechanism question, then concludes 'The practical questions are narrower than the slogans suggest'.
fast: Look for the 'deserve attention, but…' framing.
hint: Paragraph 2 opening and the last paragraph.
trap: Option C is one possibility the author raises, not the thesis.
note: Measured scepticism is a common CAT author stance.
evidence: The results deserve attention, but they also deserve scrutiny.
The practical questions are narrower than the slogans suggest

text: The author's point about firms that volunteer for trials implies that:
options: managers who volunteer are dishonest about results.
the success of the trials may not generalise to other kinds of organisations.
trial results cannot be trusted at all.
hospitals have already adopted four-day weeks.
solution: 'Their success shows that a shorter week can work in some settings; it does not show that it will work everywhere.' C and A overstate.
fast: Self-selection limits generalisation.
hint: What does a non-random sample prevent?
trap: Option C — the author says results 'deserve attention'.
note: Self-selection bias: results true for volunteers may not transfer.
evidence: it does not show that it will work everywhere

text: Which of the following findings would most weaken the defenders' claim that the shorter week acts as a 'forcing device'?
options: Staff at four-day firms reported higher satisfaction.
Four-day trial firms took fewer sick days.
Firms that cut meetings while keeping a five-day week achieved productivity gains as large as those of four-day trial firms.
Hospitals find it hard to adopt a four-day week.
solution: The defenders say reorganisation 'would never have happened without the pressure of a lost day'. If five-day firms reorganised and gained as much, the lost day was not necessary.
fast: Show the effect occurring without the supposed cause.
hint: What does 'would never have happened without' predict?
trap: Option A or B — benefits, but they don't address the mechanism.
note: To weaken a necessity claim, show the outcome without the condition.
evidence: the reorganisation would never have happened without the pressure of a lost day

text: Which of the following is NOT reported in the passage as a result claimed by participating firms?
options: Customer complaints fell sharply.
Fewer employees resigned.
Output held steady or rose.
Fewer sick days were taken.
solution: The passage lists output, sick days and resignations. Customer complaints are not mentioned (customers appear only as a question to consider).
fast: Tick off the three listed results.
trap: Choosing a listed result by skimming.
note: NOT questions: the right answer is absent from the text.
evidence: output held steady or even rose, that staff took fewer sick days, and that fewer people resigned

text: Which of the following best captures the central idea of the passage?
options: Stepwells were built mainly as religious monuments.
Stepwell restoration projects have fully revived their original purpose.
Stepwells combined a practical water function with a civic and social role, and their decline and restoration raise questions about what modern infrastructure leaves out.
Piped water was a mistake that should be reversed.
solution: 'To build a stepwell was to build a public room organised around a shared necessity.' The decline 'leaves something out', restoration 'preserves the stone but not always the purpose', and the final question is about 'infrastructure that is also a civic space'.
D overstates: the author grants that piped water 'spared people hours of labour'.
fast: The thesis connects past function, decline and a present question.
hint: Look for the 'public room' idea recurring.
trap: Option D ignores the concession about convenience.
note: Nuanced passages concede a point before adding a cost.
evidence: To build a stepwell was to build a public room organised around a shared necessity.
infrastructure that is also a civic space

text: The author's comment that a restored stepwell may be 'a museum of a social arrangement rather than the arrangement itself' suggests that:
options: museums are the best way to preserve heritage.
preserving the structure does not recreate the everyday use that gave it social meaning.
restoration is pointless.
stepwells should be closed to visitors.
solution: 'This preserves the stone but not always the purpose. A restored stepwell that no one needs to visit...' — the social use is missing.
fast: Stone vs purpose.
trap: Option C is too extreme ('not always').
note: Metaphors are usually explained by the adjacent sentence.
evidence: This preserves the stone but not always the purpose.

text: According to the passage, why did stepwells allow water to be used in every season?
options: Because patrons refilled them in summer.
Because they stored rainwater in covered tanks.
Because their steps let people reach water at whatever depth it stood as the water table rose and fell.
Because they were connected to rivers.
solution: 'a well that can be approached at any depth remains usable in every season.'
fast: Direct.
trap: Options invent mechanisms not in the passage.
note: Detail answers restate the text.
evidence: a well that can be approached at any depth remains usable in every season

text: The author's attitude towards the usual account of stepwells' decline as technological progress is best described as:
options: outright rejection
amused indifference
qualified acceptance that points to an overlooked cost
complete agreement
solution: 'in one sense it is... But the story leaves something out.'
fast: 'In one sense… But…' = qualified.
trap: Choosing 'outright rejection' by skipping the concession.
note: Concession markers signal a qualified stance.
evidence: in one sense it is
But the story leaves something out.

text: Which of the following best describes the passage?
options: A description of the routes taken by migratory birds.
An account of evidence that birds sense the magnetic field, the competing hypotheses about how, and why the question is hard.
A proof that birds navigate using iron particles in their beaks.
An argument that birds rely only on the sun and stars.
solution: The passage reports strong evidence for a magnetic sense, sets out 'Two broad hypotheses', notes they 'need not be rivals', and explains why the question is hard.
C overstates; the mechanism 'is not settled'. D contradicts the magnetic evidence.
fast: Evidence → hypotheses → difficulty.
trap: Option C presents a hypothesis as proved.
note: Science passages: separate what is shown from what is hypothesised.
evidence: The evidence for a magnetic sense is strong even though its mechanism is not settled.
Two broad hypotheses have been proposed.

text: The caged-bird experiments described in the passage establish that birds:
options: prefer to migrate at night.
use magnetic iron particles as compass needles.
detect the magnetic field through their eyes.
can use magnetic information to orient themselves, though not how they detect it.
solution: 'Such experiments show that birds can use magnetic information. They do not show how that information is detected.'
fast: What vs how.
trap: Picking one of the mechanism hypotheses (C or B).
note: Distinguish what an experiment shows from what it cannot show.
evidence: Such experiments show that birds can use magnetic information.
They do not show how that information is detected.

text: The author suggests that the two hypotheses 'need not be rivals' because:
options: a bird might use one system for the field's direction and another for its strength, and redundancy helps navigation.
birds do not actually use the magnetic field.
both have been conclusively proven.
neither hypothesis is supported by any evidence.
solution: 'A bird might use one system to sense the direction of the field and another to sense its strength... a system that can cross-check several cues is less likely to be led astray'.
fast: Two systems, two jobs.
trap: Option C contradicts 'not settled'.
note: Complementary hypotheses are a common resolution in science passages.
evidence: A bird might use one system to sense the direction of the field and another to sense its strength

text: Which finding does the passage cite in support of the light-based hypothesis?
options: Magnetic orientation in some species depends on light of particular wavelengths.
Birds hop in the direction they would fly.
Birds use coastlines as landmarks.
The Earth's field is weak.
solution: 'The second hypothesis is supported by findings that magnetic orientation in some species depends on light of particular wavelengths'.
fast: Direct.
trap: Option B supports a magnetic sense in general, not the light mechanism.
note: Match evidence to the specific claim it supports.
evidence: depends on light of particular wavelengths

text: The central argument of the passage is that:
options: forecasters are systematically overconfident, and honest statements of uncertainty are best produced by procedures that supply information intuition suppresses.
experts' forecasts are worthless and should be ignored.
psychology alone explains why forecasts fail.
averaging forecasts is always better than consulting experts.
solution: Paragraph 1 documents overconfidence; paragraphs 3–4 give procedural remedies that 'introduce information that the forecaster's own intuition tends to suppress'; the conclusion: honesty 'is more likely to be produced by procedures than by good intentions.'
B contradicts 'The broader lesson is not that experts should be ignored.'
fast: Problem + procedural remedy.
trap: Option B is explicitly denied.
note: 'The broader lesson is not X… The lesson is Y' — pick Y.
evidence: The ranges are too narrow.
more likely to be produced by procedures than by good intentions

text: Why, according to the passage, does averaging several forecasters' estimates often beat the best individual?
options: Because the best individual is usually dishonest.
Because averaging widens every range.
Because their errors partly cancel out.
Because groups are always wiser than individuals.
solution: 'Averaging the independent estimates of several forecasters often beats the best individual, because their errors partly cancel.'
D overstates ('always').
fast: Direct 'because'.
trap: Option D turns 'often' into 'always'.
note: Qualifiers (often/always) decide many RC answers.
evidence: because their errors partly cancel

text: A project manager wants her team's completion-date estimates to be better calibrated. Based on the passage, which step is most likely to help?
options: Rewarding team members whose bold estimates turn out right.
Asking each member to imagine the project has overrun and to explain why before giving a range.
Asking members to give the narrowest range they can defend.
Asking only the most senior engineer for an estimate.
solution: 'Forecasters who are asked to imagine that their prediction has failed and to explain why tend to widen their ranges.'
A reinforces the selection for confidence; C narrows ranges.
fast: Pre-mortem technique.
trap: Option A recreates the structural problem.
note: Application: map the scenario onto a named remedy.
evidence: asked to imagine that their prediction has failed and to explain why tend to widen their ranges

text: The author would most likely agree that expertise:
options: should be replaced entirely by averaging.
often improves the central estimate of a forecast even if it does not ensure an honest range.
guarantees calibrated forecasts.
is useless for forecasting.
solution: 'Expertise often improves the centre of a forecast even when it fails to widen the range.'
fast: Direct.
trap: Options D and C are opposite extremes.
note: Eliminate both extremes first.
evidence: Expertise often improves the centre of a forecast even when it fails to widen the range.

text:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

In complex fields such as surgery and aviation, experienced professionals sometimes fail not because they lack knowledge but because they skip a step they know perfectly well. Under pressure, attention narrows, and routine tasks that have been performed thousands of times are the easiest to overlook. Simple checklists, which experts often resent as insulting to their skill, have been found to reduce such errors substantially. Their value lies not in teaching anything new but in guarding against the predictable lapses of people who already know what to do.
options: Surgery and aviation are the professions most prone to error.
Experts resent checklists because checklists teach them nothing new.
Checklists help experts mainly by preventing lapses in steps they already know, especially under pressure.
Experience makes professionals more likely to lack essential knowledge.
solution: The core: failures come from skipped known steps; checklists guard against 'predictable lapses of people who already know what to do'.
B is a side detail; A is not claimed; D contradicts 'not because they lack knowledge'.
fast: Summaries keep the cause (lapses under pressure) and the remedy (checklists).
hint: What is the checklist's 'value', according to the last line?
trap: Picking B because it repeats a vivid detail.
note: A summary is not the most memorable line; it is the argument in brief.
evidence: guarding against the predictable lapses of people who already know what to do

text:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The popular idea that ten thousand hours of practice will make anyone an expert misreads the research on which it is based. What distinguished top performers in those studies was not simply the quantity of practice but its quality: focused work on specific weaknesses, immediate feedback and gradual increases in difficulty. Hours spent repeating what one already does comfortably add little. Practice, in other words, improves performance mainly when it is designed to be uncomfortable.
options: Anyone who practises for ten thousand hours will become an expert.
Improvement comes mainly from focused, feedback-rich practice aimed at weaknesses, not from accumulated hours alone.
Comfortable practice is harmful and should be avoided.
Top performers practise fewer hours than average performers.
solution: The passage corrects the 'ten thousand hours' myth: quality ('focused work on specific weaknesses, immediate feedback') matters more than quantity.
A is the misreading; D is unsupported; C overstates 'add little' as 'harmful'.
fast: Correction passages: summarise the correction, not the myth.
trap: C — 'add little' is not 'harmful'.
note: Watch for summaries that intensify the author's claims.
evidence: not simply the quantity of practice but its quality

text:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Gross domestic product measures the market value of goods and services produced in an economy, and it has become the default yardstick of national progress. Yet it counts some things that make lives worse—the cost of cleaning up after a disaster raises it—and ignores others that make lives better, such as unpaid care within families or the value of clean air. GDP was designed to measure production, not well-being, and problems arise when it is treated as a measure of the latter.
options: Unpaid care is the most important economic activity.
Disasters are good for the economy because they raise GDP.
GDP should be abolished as a statistic.
GDP is a sound measure of production but misleading as a measure of well-being, because it counts some harms and omits some goods.
solution: 'GDP was designed to measure production, not well-being, and problems arise when it is treated as a measure of the latter.'
C is extreme; A and B distort examples.
fast: The last sentence states the thesis.
trap: B twists an example into a claim.
note: Examples illustrate; they are not the summary.
evidence: GDP was designed to measure production, not well-being

text:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A forest with many tree species may grow no faster in an ordinary year than a plantation of a single species. The difference appears in bad years. When a pest or drought strikes, some species in a diverse forest are likely to cope better than others, and the forest as a whole recovers. A monoculture has no such reserve: a threat that harms one tree harms them all. Diversity, in this sense, functions less like a source of extra yield than like insurance.
options: Diverse forests grow faster than single-species plantations.
Monoculture plantations should be banned.
The main value of species diversity lies in resilience to shocks rather than in higher output in normal times.
Pests and droughts are becoming more common.
solution: 'Diversity... functions less like a source of extra yield than like insurance.'
A contradicts the first line; B is extreme; D is not stated.
fast: Insurance = protection in bad times.
hint: Read the metaphor in the last line.
trap: A ignores 'may grow no faster in an ordinary year'.
note: Summaries often paraphrase a closing metaphor.
evidence: functions less like a source of extra yield than like insurance

text:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Children are often said to learn languages effortlessly, while adults struggle. The comparison is less fair than it seems. Children spend years immersed in a language, surrounded by patient speakers and free of the fear of embarrassment; adults usually study a few hours a week in classrooms. Adults, in fact, often learn vocabulary and grammar faster in the early stages. Where children clearly excel is in acquiring a native-like accent, which becomes harder to achieve later in life.
options: Classroom teaching is useless for adult learners.
Adults can never match children in learning languages.
Children learn grammar faster than adults in every stage.
Children's apparent advantage largely reflects immersive conditions; adults may learn faster at first, though children have an edge in accent.
solution: Three points: the comparison is unfair (conditions differ), adults 'often learn vocabulary and grammar faster in the early stages', children excel at accent. Only D keeps all three.
B and A are extreme; C contradicts the passage.
fast: Complex summaries must keep the qualification about accent.
trap: Choosing an option that drops the accent point or the conditions point.
note: Complete summaries preserve contrasts and qualifications.
evidence: The comparison is less fair than it seems.
Where children clearly excel is in acquiring a native-like accent

text:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Open-plan offices were promoted as a way to encourage collaboration by removing the walls between colleagues. Studies that tracked actual behaviour after firms moved to open layouts, however, have sometimes found that face-to-face interaction fell while email and messaging rose. Deprived of privacy, workers appear to create it in other ways—by wearing headphones, avoiding conversation and retreating to digital channels. The removal of physical barriers does not automatically remove social ones.
options: Workers prefer email to conversation.
Firms should return to closed offices immediately.
Removing walls can reduce face-to-face interaction as workers seek privacy in other ways, so open layouts do not guarantee collaboration.
Open-plan offices always destroy collaboration.
solution: The finding (interaction fell), the mechanism (workers create privacy other ways) and the moral ('does not automatically remove social ones') are in C.
D turns 'sometimes' into 'always'; B is a recommendation the passage does not make.
fast: Keep 'can/does not automatically' — avoid 'always'.
hint: What do workers do when deprived of privacy?
trap: D overgeneralises 'sometimes'.
note: Hedged passages need hedged summaries.
evidence: The removal of physical barriers does not automatically remove social ones.

text:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Offering a reward for an activity can increase how often people do it, at least while the reward lasts. But when the activity was already enjoyable, a reward can change how people understand their own behaviour: they begin to see themselves as doing it for the reward. People should never be paid for work they enjoy.
Rewards increase activity permanently.
For activities people already enjoy, rewards can undermine interest once removed by changing why people think they act.

trap: Dropping the condition (A).

Newspapers report science inaccurately.

fast: Caution + mechanism.
trap: B turns 'more likely' into 'usually false'.
note: Probabilistic language should not become certainty.

Choose the sentence that most appropriately fills the blank (______) in the paragraph below.

For centuries, the only way to preserve a piece of music was to write it down or to teach it to someone else. Recording changed this. A performance could now be kept exactly as it happened, including the hesitations and accidents that notation leaves out. ______
options: For the first time, a particular performance, and not only the composition, could become the lasting work.
As a result, musicians stopped writing music down altogether.
Recordings are always better than live performances.
Teaching music to others soon became unnecessary.
solution: The paragraph contrasts preserving compositions (notation) with preserving performances (recording). A draws that consequence.
B, C, D are extreme.
fast: Complete the contrast notation vs recording.
hint: What could be preserved that notation leaves out?
trap: Extreme consequences (stopped altogether, always better).
note: Eliminate absolute options first.
evidence: A performance could now be kept exactly as it happened

Choose the sentence that most appropriately fills the blank (______) in the paragraph below.

The fastest-growing plants are not always the ones that dominate a landscape in the long run. ______ Slower-growing species that invest in deep roots and tough wood may be overtaken at first, but they survive the droughts and storms that eventually cut the fast growers down.
options: Plant growth is controlled mainly by the amount of sunlight received.
Farmers prefer fast-growing crops for obvious economic reasons.
Deep roots are found only in desert plants.
Rapid growth often comes at the cost of durability, leaving fast growers vulnerable when hard times arrive.
solution: The blank must explain why fast growers may lose: a trade-off between speed and durability. D provides it and sets up the next sentence.
fast: Look for the trade-off that the next sentence illustrates.
hint: What do slow growers invest in instead?
trap: B drifts to agriculture.
note: Middle blanks must fit both neighbours.
evidence: invest in deep roots and tough wood

text:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide in which blank (option 1, 2, 3 or 4) the following sentence would best fit.

Sentence: Amid this generosity, however, few of the people receiving the aid were ever asked what they actually needed.

Paragraph: After the flood, aid arrived quickly from many directions. ___(1)___ Trucks brought blankets, bottled water and tinned food, and volunteers set up kitchens in school buildings. ___(2)___ Villagers who had lost their seed stock and tools found themselves with more blankets than they could use and nothing with which to replant their fields. ___(3)___ Relief that is generous but uninformed can leave the most important losses untouched. ___(4)___
options: Option 1
Option 2
Option 3
Option 4
solution: 'This generosity' refers to the specific aid described (trucks, kitchens), so the sentence must come after it. It then explains the mismatch that follows (blankets but no seeds). Blank 2.
fast: 'This generosity' needs the detailed description first.
hint: What does 'this generosity' point back to?
trap: Blank 1 — the generosity has not yet been described in detail.
note: Demonstratives need a concrete antecedent just before them.
evidence: Trucks brought blankets, bottled water and tinned food

Choose the sentence that most appropriately fills the blank (______) in the paragraph below.

Many ancient buildings have survived earthquakes that destroyed newer structures nearby. Engineers studying them have found that their builders often used techniques that allowed walls to shift slightly without collapsing: layers of flexible material between stones, interlocking joints, and foundations that could slide. ______
options: Earthquakes were probably less powerful in ancient times.
All new buildings should therefore be made of stone.
Rigidity, it seems, is not always the best defence against shaking ground; controlled flexibility can be safer.
Ancient builders must therefore have understood modern physics.
solution: The evidence (techniques allowing walls to shift) supports C. D overreaches; B misidentifies the key factor (flexibility, not stone); A is unsupported.
fast: Generalise the mechanism described.
hint: What did the techniques allow walls to do?
trap: B fixes on the material instead of the principle.
note: The completion should generalise, not overreach.
evidence: allowed walls to shift slightly without collapsing
